#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PreToolUse guard: nothing authored from a Claude session carries AI
attribution when it is written the ordinary way.

Rule (.claude/rules/git.md): commits, PR titles and bodies, issue bodies,
comments, reviews, releases and tags belong to the maintainer. The harness
can inject a note asking for attribution trailers; this hook is the
mechanical answer so the note can never win.

The contract is "no attribution", not "no mention". Denied: a Co-Authored-By
naming an AI, an Anthropic noreply address, "Generated with / written by
<AI>", a line ending "via Claude Code" or "by Claude", a Claude Code session
link or Claude-Session trailer, a session id, "AI-assisted / AI-generated"
and the robot emoji. Plain mentions pass: "fix the Claude Code hook config",
"compatible with Claude Code", "integration with LLM providers", CLAUDE.md,
the repo's own name, a human Co-Authored-By.

What is scanned, for any git write, gh write or GitHub API call:
  * The full command text: inline -m / --body / --title / --notes values,
    here-docs, here-strings and PowerShell -Body all live there.
  * Every file a command names with a body flag (-F / --file / --template
    for a git write, -F at the end of a cluster (-aF), and -t for git
    commit; --body-file / --notes-file / --input / -F and
    --field key=@file; -d @file and -F key=@file; -InFile; Get-Content's
    path). Bindwright's helper parses the command the way the shell does
    (`hooks/shell-words.mjs`), so each flag belongs to one
    command. A brace of plain text is read both as text built at run time
    and as the words bash makes of it (`{-F,msg.txt}` as `-F msg.txt`),
    since a shell may or may not expand it. Every command's flags are read, a wrapper's (`env`, `sudo`,
    `xargs`) included, except a text tool's (`awk -F,`, `grep -F word`),
    git's in a read (`git log -F`), and gh's `--template`. A flag inside
    quoted text, a here-doc, a here-string or the value of -m / --body /
    --title is text, not a body file. A relative path is read in the start
    folder and in every folder a `cd` (`builtin cd` and `command cd` too),
    `pushd`, `Set-Location`, `git -C` or `env -C` / `--chdir` in the
    command names, each reached from the folders named before it in
    the text, since one may run in a child shell or fail, then again until
    no folder is added, since a loop or a function may run one again. One
    after a folder change it cannot place (`cd -`, a
    target built at run time, a folder this computer cannot find) is
    denied. A file it cannot read, or one named by text built at run time,
    is denied, so a typo cannot slip a body through unread. A program built
    at run time has every file flag of its command read. A shell's options
    are never read: each argument of `bash`, `sh`, `zsh` and the like whose
    text names a write or a hook change is parsed and read like the command,
    up to three shells deep; one built at run time or nested deeper is
    denied, as is a nested `pwsh` or `powershell` whose text arguments name
    one, since PowerShell joins them into a script (but a script block
    after options alone is read with the command, and words after a `.ps1`
    file are its parameters). A shell named at run time, or a word after
    git, gh or a text tool first or after `sudo`-like wrappers, is not read.

The parser is required: it runs on Node 18 or later from Bindwright's
helper, which setup installs with this guard. A command this hook reads is
denied when either is missing, when the helper is older than this hook, or
when the parser cannot read the command (an array built at run time,
PowerShell's `--%`, syntax it rejects), with a reason that names the fix.

Also denied, since the hook cannot see past them, for a git program (a
word built at run time that names git, such as `$GIT`, counts as one): a
write that skips git's own hooks (`--no-verify`, `-n` on commit or am),
setting or unsetting `core.hooksPath` or a `hook.` setting (`git config`,
`-c`, `--config-env`; reading one passes), `--trailer`, a commit that
reuses another commit's message (`-C`, `-c`, `--reuse-message`,
`--reedit-message`), and turning lefthook off (`LEFTHOOK=0` or `false` set
by the command, `lefthook uninstall`), and a git call whose subcommand
comes from a word built at run time with no literal word other than an
option written right after it (`git "${args[@]}"`, `git "$@" -m x`,
PowerShell's `git @args`), or from a word before it that may become several
(`git -C "$@"`, `git --namespace="$@"`) unless only git's own options stand
between that word and a subcommand written out (`git -C $d --no-pager log`). Options are read as git reads them, bundled
(`-nm x`) or shortened (`--no-veri`), so a message that names one passes.
A word built at run time counts for the literal text around its run-time
parts (`--trailer=$WHO`, `"-C$SHA"`, `"$S.hooksPath"`), and one
that can expand to no word (`$OPTS`, `"$@"`) is also read as absent.

It is a safety net for attribution written the ordinary way, not a sandbox
against a command built to slip past it. No text check can be one. These
pass unread: message text the shell builds at run time ($VAR, $(...),
backticks, eval), a body file the command itself writes, a body piped in
on stdin, a git alias or a git program built at run time whose text does
not name git (their options are not read as git's), an option, setting or
`git config` name whose text the shell builds at run time (`${X:+-n}`,
`$(echo --no-verify)`, `"$KEY"`, `core.ho$'o'ksPath`), a body-file flag
the shell builds at run time from a word that does not start with `-` as
written (`$F` holding `-F msg.txt`), a script PowerShell decodes
(`-EncodedCommand`), a git named at run time whose subcommand is built too
(`$GIT "$@"`), one inside `bash -c` whose subcommand is built, one built
at run time and followed right away by a literal word such as a pathspec
(`git "$@" .`), one with a built subcommand behind a program other than
the shell's wrappers and the common runners (`flock f git "$@"`; `sudo`,
`env`, `timeout`, `stdbuf` and the like are read), a write whose text a
redirection holding `&` splits
(`git 2>&1 commit`, `git 2>&1 "$@"`), and text a program
started by the command writes on its own. The repo's `attribution` settings
switch off the harness's own trailers; this hook catches the ones written
by hand.

Its reading lives in the no_ai_attribution/ folder beside it, which ships
and installs with it. The repo registers this file through run-hook.sh, which skips it when
~/.claude/hooks/no-ai-attribution.py exists and ~/.claude/settings.json
names it outside a permission rule.

Exit contract: JSON permissionDecision=deny on stdout, exit 0. Silent
exit 0 otherwise. A read-only command is blocked only for the routes above,
or when the parser it needs is missing or cannot read it.
"""
import importlib.util
import json
import os
import re
import sys
import time


# Obfuscation-tolerant: optional zero-width / separator chars between letters.
_Z = r"[​‌‍⁠﻿\s\-_.*]*"


def _fuzzy(word):
    return _Z.join(re.escape(ch) for ch in word)


CLAUDE = _fuzzy("claude")
ANTHROPIC = _fuzzy("anthropic")
# Tool names that make a phrase attribution. `cursor` alone is an ordinary UI
# word ("pointer with cursor"), so only "Cursor AI / IDE / agent" counts.
AI = (r"(?:" + CLAUDE + "|" + ANTHROPIC + r"|ai|llm|assistant|copilot|codex|chat" + _Z + r"gpt|gpt|gemini|"
      r"cursor" + _Z + r"(?:ai|ide|agent))")
AN = r"(?:an?" + _Z + r")?"

# Bindwright's own Attribution workflow imports ATTRIBUTION and strip_paths from
# this file: keep both names, and keep importing it free of side effects (main()
# runs only as a script).
ATTRIBUTION = re.compile(
    "|".join([
        # Co-Authored-By naming an AI; a human co-author passes.
        # No two separator runs touch: `-` is one of them, and two in a row make a long run of
        # separators take time that grows with its length squared. For the same reason the
        # blank lines after `by` and the rest of its line are two runs that share no character.
        r"co" + _Z + r"authored" + _Z + r"by(?:\s*\n)?[^\n]*?\b" + AI + r"\b",
        r"noreply@" + ANTHROPIC,
        r"\b(?:generated|written|created|made|authored|produced|assisted|co-?written)" + _Z
        + r"(?:with|by|using|via)" + _Z + r"(?::" + _Z + r")?" + AN + AI + r"\b",
        # Trailer forms with a colon: "Assisted-by: <AI>:<model>", "Made-with: Cursor".
        r"\b(?:generated|written|created|made|authored|produced|assisted|co-?written)" + _Z
        + r"(?:with|by|using|via)" + _Z + r":[ \t]*" + AN + r"(?:" + AI + r"|cursor)\b",
        # A line or quoted message that ends "via Claude Code" / "by Claude".
        # Not "with" / "using": "compatible with Claude Code" is a mention.
        r"\b(?:by|via)" + _Z + CLAUDE + r"(?:" + _Z + r"code)?(?=[\s.!)\]]*(?:$|['\"`]))",
        r"claude\.(?:ai|com)/(?:code|claude-code)\b",
        r"\b" + CLAUDE + r"[-_]session\s*:",
        r"session_[0-9a-z]{20,}",
        r"\U0001F916",                       # robot emoji
        r"\bai" + _Z + r"(?:assisted|generated|written|authored)",
    ]), re.I | re.M)
# A subcommand is a whole word: one inside a path or a name (`.claude/hooks/push-guard.py`,
# `commit-msg`) names no write.
_WORD_START = r"(?<![\w./\\:-])"
_WORD_END = r"(?![\w./-])"
# One command of a line: the text between `|`, `;`, `&` and line ends.
_SEGMENT = re.compile(r"[^|;&\n]+")


def _in_order(*patterns):
    """A test of text: each pattern matches after the one before it, inside one segment. The
    earliest match of each is enough, so it runs in linear time, where one pattern joined by
    lazy runs takes time that grows with the cube of a long line's length."""
    compiled = [re.compile(p, re.I) for p in patterns]

    def test(text):
        for segment in _SEGMENT.finditer(text):
            at = segment.start()
            for pattern in compiled:
                hit = pattern.search(text, at, segment.end())
                if not hit:
                    break
                at = hit.end()
            else:
                return True
        return False
    return test


def _word(alternatives):
    return _WORD_START + "(?:" + alternatives + ")" + _WORD_END


GIT_WRITE = _in_order(r"\bgit\b", _word(
    "commit-tree|commit|merge|push|tag|notes|am|cherry-pick|revert|rebase|replace"))
GH_WRITE = _in_order(r"\bgh\b", _word("pr|issue|release|gist|repo"),
                     _word("create|edit|comment|review|merge|close|reopen"))
# A git call that may take its subcommand from a word built at run time (`git "${args[@]}"`,
# PowerShell's `git @args`): a `$` or backtick anywhere after git (`--namespace="$@"`), or a word
# starting with `@` or `(`. It only sends the command to the parser, whose reading decides; a
# command the parser cannot read is not refused for it.
GIT_BUILT = _in_order(r"\bgit(?:\.(?:exe|cmd|bat|com))?\b", r"[$`]|[ \t][\"']?[@(]")
GH_API = _in_order(r"\bgh\b", _word("api"))
HTTP_GH = _in_order(r"\b(?:curl|Invoke-(?:RestMethod|WebRequest))\b", r"api\.github\.com")
# Commands that may change which hooks run without writing anything.
GIT_CONFIG_HOOKS = _in_order(r"\bgit\b", r"\bconfig\b", r"hook|--re[mn]|\bre(?:move|name)-section\b")
LEFTHOOK_SET = re.compile(r"\blefthook\b\W*=", re.I)
LEFTHOOK_UNINSTALL = _in_order(r"\blefthook\b", r"\buninstall\b")
# A line end the shell joins to the next: `\` (an even run of `\` escapes itself) or
# PowerShell's backtick after a blank.
CONTINUED_LINE = re.compile(r"(?<!\\)((?:\\\\)*)\\\r?\n|(?<=[ \t])`\r?\n")
# Text bash rewrites before a program sees it: a backslash escape or an ANSI-C or locale
# string can spell any word, so the text checks cannot rule such a command out.
SHELL_ESCAPES = re.compile(r"\\|\$['\"]")

PATH_TOKEN = re.compile(r"(?<!:/)(?<![\w])(?:[A-Za-z]:|~)?(?:[\\/][\w.\-]+)+")
ALL_PARSES_SECONDS = 9  # every parse of one command, nested strings included: the hook is stopped at 10 s
BYPASS_REASONS = {
    "hooks": "git hook bypass (--no-verify / -n) is not allowed.",
    "setting": ("setting core.hooksPath or a hook. setting changes which hooks git runs;"
                " ask the user to run it."),
    "trailer": "--trailer is not allowed; write the message body directly.",
    "reuse": "reusing another commit's message (-C / -c / --reuse-message) cannot be scanned.",
    "lefthook": "turning lefthook off removes the commit-msg attribution check.",
    "unread": ("this git call has more words built at run time than the guard reads every way;"
               " split it, or write some of them out."),
    "built": ("this git call takes its subcommand from a word built at run time (`git \"${args[@]}\"`),"
              " which may hold a commit and its options; write the subcommand out."),
}


def deny(reason):
    sys.stdout.write(json.dumps({
        "hookSpecificOutput": {
            "hookEventName": "PreToolUse", "permissionDecision": "deny",
            "permissionDecisionReason": "BLOCKED (no AI attribution): " + reason
                + " Commits, PRs, issues, comments and releases belong to the maintainer; no AI "
                  "Co-Authored-By, no generated-with line, no session link, no robot emoji.",
        }
    }))
    sys.exit(0)


def strip_paths(text):
    """Mask file-system paths so a scratch directory named after a session
    cannot trip the scan. URLs survive (the lookbehind skips the `//` after a
    scheme), so session links are still caught."""
    return PATH_TOKEN.sub("<path>", text)


def scan_text(text, where):
    hit = ATTRIBUTION.search(strip_paths(text))
    if hit:
        deny(f"attribution marker '{hit.group(0).strip()}' found in {where}.")


def routes_in(text):
    """(writes, names a route, may build git's subcommand): whether text names a git or GitHub
    write, a hook change, or a git call with a word built at run time after it, as written, with
    line ends joined, and without quotes (`com'mit'`) or escapes (`g\\it`)."""
    joined = CONTINUED_LINE.sub(r"\1", text)
    texts = (text, joined, re.sub(r"[\"'`]", "", joined), re.sub(r"[\"'`\\]", "", joined))
    writes = any(test(t) for test in (GIT_WRITE, GH_WRITE, GH_API, HTTP_GH) for t in texts)
    named = writes or any(test(t) for test in (GIT_CONFIG_HOOKS, LEFTHOOK_SET.search, LEFTHOOK_UNINSTALL)
                          for t in texts)
    return writes, named, any(GIT_BUILT(t) for t in texts)


def readers(named):
    """The package's readers, loaded only here so the Attribution workflow can import this file
    alone; without the package, a command that names a route is refused, as without the parser."""
    sys.dont_write_bytecode = True  # no __pycache__ beside a hook a repo may commit
    here = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)).replace("\\", "/")
    # Loaded by its own path, never through sys.path, so no other file beside the hook can stand
    # in for a module the guard imports.
    folder = os.path.join(here, "no_ai_attribution")
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(
        "no_ai_attribution", os.path.join(folder, "__init__.py"), submodule_search_locations=[folder])
    try:
        package = sys.modules["no_ai_attribution"] = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
        spec.loader.exec_module(package)
        package.routes_in = routes_in
        from no_ai_attribution.files import parsed_files
        from no_ai_attribution.routes import hook_route
        from no_ai_attribution.shell import parse, with_nested
    except (ImportError, OSError):
        if named:
            deny("the folder no_ai_attribution/ beside this guard, which reads the command, is missing."
                 " Copy it back from Bindwright's helper: `cp -r ~/.bindwright/helper/node_modules/bindwright"
                 f"/_core/global-template/hooks/no_ai_attribution \"{here}/\"` (`helper/python/bindwright`"
                 " after a pip install), or `git checkout -- .claude/hooks/no_ai_attribution` where the"
                 " repo commits it.")
        sys.exit(0)
    return parse, with_nested, parsed_files, hook_route


def parse_reason(cmd, shell, named, built):
    """Why a command goes to the parser: "routes" when its text names a route or it is an
    escaped bash command, "built" when it only may build git's subcommand, None when it does not.
    An escaped command is refused only for what the parser's words show, so a parser that cannot
    read it refuses nothing new; a "built" one is refused only for a built subcommand."""
    if named or shell == "bash" and SHELL_ESCAPES.search(cmd):
        return "routes"
    return "built" if built else None


def main():
    try:
        data = json.loads(sys.stdin.buffer.read().decode("utf-8-sig"))
    except Exception:
        sys.exit(0)
    tool_input = data.get("tool_input") if isinstance(data, dict) else None
    cmd = tool_input.get("command") if isinstance(tool_input, dict) else None
    if not isinstance(cmd, str):
        sys.exit(0)  # not a shell call this guard can read: let it through
    cwd = data.get("cwd")
    if not isinstance(cwd, str) or not cwd:
        cwd = os.getcwd()
    writes, named, built = routes_in(cmd)
    shell = "powershell" if data.get("tool_name") == "PowerShell" else "bash"
    reason = parse_reason(cmd, shell, named, built)
    if not reason:
        sys.exit(0)
    parse, with_nested, parsed_files, hook_route = readers(named)

    if writes:
        scan_text(cmd, "the command text")
    deadline = time.monotonic() + ALL_PARSES_SECONDS
    parsed, assignments, problem = parse(cmd, shell, cwd, deadline)
    found = []  # A nested string is read only when it names a route, so its problems all refuse.
    if not problem:
        groups, assignments, problem = with_nested(parsed, assignments, shell, cwd, deadline, found)
    if problem:
        if named or found:
            deny(problem)
        sys.exit(0)
    for text in (t for t in found if routes_in(t)[0]):
        writes = True
        scan_text(text, "a command string a shell runs")
    # A command that writes nothing is checked only for the routes past the hooks.
    for path, error in (parsed_files(groups, cwd) if writes else ()):
        if error:
            deny(f"could not tell which file holds {error}. Use a literal absolute path.")
        try:
            text = open(path, encoding="utf-8-sig", errors="replace").read()
        except Exception as e:
            deny(f"could not read message/body file {path}: {e}. Use a literal absolute path.")
        scan_text(text, f"file {path}")
    route = hook_route(groups, assignments, reason == "built")
    if route:
        deny(BYPASS_REASONS[route])
    sys.exit(0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

routes_in = None
files..claude/hooks/push-guard.py:
r"""PreToolUse hook: block force pushes that permission rules cannot see.

Permission rules match command text, so `-f` bundled with other short flags
(`-qf`, `-vf`, `-uqf`) escapes them. This hook reads the text of every Bash
and PowerShell command and blocks a git push that carries:

- `--force` or `-f`, alone or inside a short-flag bundle;
- `--mirror` (or a prefix of it), which force-updates and deletes every
  remote ref;
- a refspec starting with `+`, a force push of that one ref;
- `-c remote.<name>.push=+...` or a true `-c remote.<name>.mirror`;
- a one-off alias for push (`git -c alias.p='push -f' p`).

`--force-with-lease` and `--force-if-includes` stay allowed: they refuse to
overwrite work the local repo has not seen. The same checks cover git's push
plumbing, `send-pack` and `http-push`, and the dashed `git-push` programs.

It is a safety net for force pushes written the ordinary way, not a sandbox
against a command built to slip past it: no text check can be one, since a
program started by the command can push on its own.

The hook reads text, not shell grammar. First it removes what the shell
would remove: line continuations, quotes, backslashes and backticks,
decoding Bash's `$'...'` escapes when the string closes on its own line
(the result stays one word) and PowerShell's `` `u{...} `` on the way. Each
command substitution (`$(...)`, `$((...))`, `${...}`, `<(...)`, a Bash
backtick pair on one line, a PowerShell `(...)`) is read on its own. In the
text around it, a substitution inside a word joins the text on both sides
(`-q$(true)f` reads as `-qf`) and one at a word's edge leaves a word; a
PowerShell group of quoted literals (`@('push','-qf')`) stays in place as
arguments. The rest is cut into
statements at every newline, and at every `;`, `|` and `&` that is neither
escaped nor inside a quoted string that closes on its own line (in
PowerShell also at `{` and `}`). Redirects and their targets are dropped,
except a target that names git (`bash <<< "git push -f"`). After a `git`
word, a later push word in the same statement starts the push, and the
words after it are its arguments. Text inside `eval`, `sh -c`,
`pwsh -Command`, a heredoc or a comment is read the same way. Each shell's
own line continuation is removed. Git Bash drops every carriage return first,
so a Bash command holding one is also read without them. Bash keeps a `\`
ending a comment, a single-quoted line or a quoted heredoc line as a line
end instead, so a Bash command with a `\` ending a line is read whole: with
each such `\` joined and with it kept as a line end, and each reading also
as one statement, so a push anywhere in it with a force word anywhere after
it blocks. Every step is linear in the command's length.

That includes text that only mentions a force push: a commit message, a
script or a search pattern with `git push -f` in it is blocked too. So is a
plain push in a Bash command with a `\` ending a line when a force word
follows anywhere in it (`git push origin main \` then `&& rm -rf build`). A
plain push chained after a quoted string that spans lines can block the same
way: on the string's last line its closing quote pairs with the next quote,
so the flag of a later statement there (`rm -rf`) reads as the push's. The
block message says to put such text in a file and pass the file instead,
and to put a command with a `\` ending a line on one line or run its push as
a command of its own.

The hook only ever blocks or stays silent; it never asks. Out of reach, so
these run without a block:

- a force flag the shell builds at run time (`git push $FLAGS`,
  `$(echo -qf)`, `xargs`, brace expansion, text piped into a shell or
  `iex`, `('-q'+'f')`, PowerShell's `-f` format operator as in
  `("+{0}" -f $b)`, PowerShell's `--%`);
- git config or aliases that force a later plain `git push`, whether on
  disk (`git config alias.p 'push -f'`, a `remote.<name>.push` or `mirror`
  setting) or set in the same command (`GIT_CONFIG_*` variables,
  `--config-env`);
- git reached by another name: a variable (`G=git; $G push -f`; `$GIT` and
  `${GIT:-git}` are read as git), a shell alias or `Set-Alias`, `hash -p`,
  or a glob (`gi[t]`);
- remote branch and tag deletions, and a branch deleted and then pushed
  again;
- a push run by another program (`python -c`, `node -e`, `make`, `gh api`,
  `git fetch --upload-pack`);
- a push after a git option value with spaces in it, one of whose later
  words is exactly a git subcommand in OTHER_SUBCOMMANDS (`git -C "My notes
  dir" push -f`): the search for the push word stops there;
- shell syntax this reading takes differently from the shell, where that
  cuts a push off from its `git` word or its force flag: quotes paired
  differently (a quoted string that spans lines, a `$(`, `${` or backtick
  inside single quotes, as in `echo '$('; git push origin main ')' -f`), or
  parentheses left unbalanced inside a substitution;
- a command over MAX_COMMAND characters.

Project deny rules cover some of these by text (`git remote *--mi*`, `gh repo
sync *--force*`). Input that is not JSON, or holds no command string, lets
the call through; an error inside the check refuses it.

It runs from one of two places. Installed in `~/.claude/hooks/`, setup
registers it in `~/.claude/settings.json` only after finding a Python 3.8+
interpreter outside any virtual environment, naming both the interpreter and
this file by absolute path, in exec form (`command` plus `args`), so no shell
and no `python3`/`python`/`py` guess is involved. Shipped in a repo's
`.claude/hooks/`, the committed settings start it through `run-hook.sh`,
which cannot know an absolute interpreter path: it takes the first of
`python3`, `python` and `py` that is Python 3.8+ outside a virtual
environment, and skips this file when `~/.claude/hooks/push-guard.py`
exists and `~/.claude/settings.json` names it outside a permission
rule. A project that ships it this way must keep a code indexer's hook global:
an indexer that copies the launcher of a project's existing hooks into its own
project entries, and `sh run-hook.sh` is no launcher for it.
Either way it runs through a `runpy` one-liner instead of
`python <path>` because Python exits 2 when it cannot open a script, which
would block every call. Both launchers test that the file exists first, so a
missing file lets the call proceed. The interpreter runs with `-I`, so the
project directory (the hook's working directory) is not on the import path and a
repo's own `json.py` cannot replace the modules this file imports.
"""
import json
import re
import sys

# Longer commands pass unread. Every step below is linear in the command's
# length, so this only bounds the work; no real push command comes near it.
MAX_COMMAND = 100000
# Innermost substitutions are cut out one nesting level per pass.
MAX_PASSES = 64

PUSH_SUBCOMMANDS = {"push", "send-pack", "http-push"}
PUSH_PROGRAMS = {"git-push", "git-send-pack", "git-http-push"}
# git subcommands that never push; after one, a later push word is its text.
OTHER_SUBCOMMANDS = {
    "add", "am", "apply", "archive", "bisect", "blame", "branch", "bundle", "cat-file", "checkout",
    "cherry-pick", "clean", "clone", "commit", "config", "describe", "diff", "fetch", "for-each-ref",
    "format-patch", "gc", "grep", "help", "init", "log", "ls-files", "ls-remote", "merge", "mv",
    "notes", "pull", "rebase", "reflog", "remote", "reset", "restore", "rev-list", "rev-parse",
    "revert", "rm", "shortlog", "show", "stash", "status", "submodule", "switch", "tag", "worktree"}
# git's own options that take the next word as their value; that word is
# never the subcommand (`git -C ../notes push -f`).
GIT_VALUE_OPTIONS = {"-C", "-c", "--git-dir", "--work-tree", "--namespace", "--exec-path",
                     "--super-prefix", "--config-env", "--attr-source"}

CONTINUATION = {"Bash": re.compile(r"\\\n"), "PowerShell": re.compile(r"`(?:\r\n|\n|\r)")}
# A `$'...'` string, found after skipping escapes and quoted strings the way
# `mask_quoted` pairs them, so the `$'` ending `grep 'main$'` starts nothing.
ANSI_QUOTE = re.compile(r"\\.|\"(?:[^\"\\\n]|\\.)*\"|'[^'\n]*'|\$'((?:[^'\\\n]|\\[^\n])*)'", re.S)
# Bash's `$'...'` escapes: hex, `\u` and `\U` with as few digits as Bash
# takes, octal, control characters, and single letters.
ANSI_ESCAPE = re.compile(
    r"\\(?:x([0-9A-Fa-f]{1,2})|u([0-9A-Fa-f]{1,4})|U([0-9A-Fa-f]{1,8})|([0-7]{1,3})|c(.)|(.))", re.S)
ANSI_LETTERS = {"a": "\a", "b": "\b", "e": "\x1b", "E": "\x1b", "f": "\f", "n": "\n", "r": "\r",
                "t": "\t", "v": "\v", "\\": "\\", "'": "'", "\"": "\"", "?": "?"}
# What a decoded `$'...'` holds is one word to the shell around it, so its
# separators and quotes never split or pair anything there.
ANSI_SEPARATORS = re.compile(r"[;|&\n\r{}\"'`]")
POWERSHELL_CHAR = re.compile(r"`u\{([0-9A-Fa-f]{1,6})\}")
# A parenthesis, or `case`/`esac` where Bash reads it as a keyword: at a
# command's start (`x=$(case ...`, `; case`, `then case`), never as an
# argument (`echo in case`, `--ignore-case`).
CASE_TOKEN = re.compile(r"[$<>]?\(|\)|(?:^|(?<=[;&|({\n])|(?<=\bthen)|(?<=\bdo)|(?<=\belse))[ \t]*case(?=\s)"
                        r"|(?<![^\s;&|])esac(?![^\s;&|)])", re.M)
# PowerShell runs any `(...)` as its own expression (`("v{0}" -f $n)`).
# Bash arithmetic `$((...))` is cut out whole, so its `+` is no refspec; a
# bare `(...)` (a subshell, an arithmetic group) is cut out on its own. A
# group that still holds a `$(` or `${` waits a pass, so the innermost
# substitution is always cut first (`("${TICKET}-fix")`).
_PARENS = r"([^()$]*(?:\$(?![({])[^()$]*)*)"
_BRACES = r"([^{}$]*(?:\$(?![({])[^{}$]*)*)"
INNERMOST = {"Bash": re.compile(r"\$\(\(" + _PARENS + r"\)\)|[$<>]?\(" + _PARENS + r"\)|\$\{" + _BRACES + r"\}"),
             "PowerShell": re.compile(r"[$@]?\(" + _PARENS + r"\)|\$\{" + _BRACES + r"\}")}
BACKTICK_GROUP = re.compile(r"`([^`\n]*)`")
# A PowerShell group of quoted literals, `@('push', '--force')`: its words are
# the command's own arguments.
LITERAL_GROUP = re.compile(r"\s*(?:'[^'\n]*'|\"[^\"$`\n]*\")(?:\s*,\s*(?:'[^'\n]*'|\"[^\"$`\n]*\"))*\s*")
# An escaped character outside quotes, a quote, or a line end.
QUOTE_OR_LINE = {"Bash": re.compile(r"\\.|[\"'\n]", re.S), "PowerShell": re.compile(r"`.|[\"'\n]", re.S)}
# A quoted string from its opening quote to a close on the same line.
QUOTED = {"Bash": {"\"": re.compile(r"\"(?:[^\"\\\n]|\\.)*\""), "'": re.compile(r"'[^'\n]*'")},
          "PowerShell": {"\"": re.compile(r"\"(?:[^\"`\n]|`.)*\""), "'": re.compile(r"'[^'\n]*'")}}
# A lone carriage return and a brace end a statement only in PowerShell
# (`{ git push -u origin x } else { Write-Host 'skip' -f Yellow }`).
STATEMENT_END = {"Bash": re.compile(r"[\n;|&]"), "PowerShell": re.compile(r"[\n\r;|&{}]")}
# The statement ends that a quote or an escape turns into plain text.
QUOTED_SEPARATORS = {"Bash": re.compile(r"[;|&]"), "PowerShell": re.compile(r"[;|&{}]")}
WORD_SPLIT = re.compile(r"[\s<>,]+")
# A redirect operator and its target, read once quotes are gone. A target
# never starts with `-` or `+`, so `--repo=">" -qf` and `-o "x>" +main` keep
# their force words.
REDIRECT = re.compile(r"(?<![0-9])[0-9]*(?:&>>?|>&|<&|>>?\|?|<)[ \t]*((?:[^\s;|&<>\-+][^\s;|&<>]*)?)")
EDGE = "(){}[]$&!@"
QUOTE_CHARS = "\"'‘’“”"
# git push has no upper-case short option, and a bundle with one fails before
# anything is pushed, so `-Leaf` and `-Filter` are not push flags.
SHORT_OPTIONS = re.compile(r"-[a-z0-9]+")
LONG_FORCE = re.compile(r"--force(?:=.*)?|--m(?:i(?:r(?:r(?:o(?:r)?)?)?)?)?")
# git reads a mirror value as true unless it is false, no, off or a zero
# number (`mirror=2` and `mirror=1k` are true). An empty value counts as
# true here: it is what is left of a quoted value with a leading space
# (`"remote.origin.mirror= 1"`).
FORCING_CONFIG = re.compile(
    r"remote\..+\.push=\+.*|remote\..+\.mirror(?:=(?!(?:false|no|off|[-+]?(?:0x)?0+[kmg]?)$).*)?", re.I)
# A `!` alias may run the dashed program, by name or path (`!git-push -f`).
PUSH_ALIAS = re.compile(
    r"alias\.[^=]+=(?:push|send-pack|http-push|!(?:\S*/)?(?:git-)?(?:push|send-pack|http-push))", re.I)


def ansi_char(match):
    """One `$'...'` escape as Bash decodes it; an unknown one stays as it is."""
    hex_code, short, long, octal, control, letter = match.groups()
    code = hex_code or short or long
    if code:
        return chr(min(int(code, 16), 0x10FFFF))
    if octal:
        return chr(int(octal, 8) & 0xFF)
    if control is not None:
        return chr(ord(control) & 0x1F)
    return ANSI_LETTERS.get(letter, "\\" + letter)


def ansi_decode(match):
    """The text of Bash's `$'...'`, decoded, as one word; anything else the
    pattern skipped stays as it is."""
    if match.group(1) is None:
        return match.group(0)
    return ANSI_SEPARATORS.sub(" ", ANSI_ESCAPE.sub(ansi_char, match.group(1)))


def neutral_cases(text):
    """The text with each `)` that ends a Bash `case` pattern turned into a
    space, so it never closes a substitution around it. A `)` that closes a
    `(`, `$(`, `<(` or `>(` opened after the `case` stays, so substitutions
    inside a case arm are read like any other."""
    out, last, stack, cases = [], 0, [], 0
    for match in CASE_TOKEN.finditer(text):
        token = match.group(0).lstrip(" \t")
        if token == "case":
            stack.append(token)
            cases += 1
        elif token == "esac":
            if cases:
                while stack.pop() != "case":
                    pass
                cases -= 1
        elif token != ")":
            stack.append("(")
        elif stack and stack[-1] == "(":
            stack.pop()
        elif stack:
            out += [text[last:match.start()], " "]
            last = match.end()
    out.append(text[last:])
    return "".join(out)


def stand_in(match, literal=False):
    """What a substitution leaves in the text around it: a PowerShell group
    of quoted literals as it is (`@('push','-qf')`), `git` when it names git
    (`& ("git") push`, `$(which git) push`), otherwise a plain word. A
    substitution inside a word joins the text on both sides (`-q$(true)f`
    reads as `-qf`); one at a word's edge leaves a word there (`+$(git
    branch)` and `"+${BRANCH}"` read as `+x`)."""
    inner = next(g for g in match.groups() if g is not None)
    if literal:
        return f" {inner} "
    text, start, end = match.string, match.start(), match.end()
    # A quote that opens or closes the word is its edge: `-C "${REPO}"` leaves
    # a word, `"${USER}-feature"` reads as `x-feature`, `-q"$(true)"f` as `-qf`.
    # So is the `(` or `,` before it and the `)` or `,` after it in a
    # PowerShell group (`("${TICKET}-fix")` reads as `x-fix`).
    before, after = start - 1, end
    while before >= 0 and text[before] in QUOTE_CHARS:
        before -= 1
    while after < len(text) and text[after] in QUOTE_CHARS:
        after += 1
    left = before >= 0 and not text[before].isspace() and text[before] not in "(,"
    right = after < len(text) and not text[after].isspace() and text[after] not in "),"
    if re.search(r"(?i)\bgit(?:\.exe)?\s*$", unquote(inner, "path")):
        word = "git"
    else:
        word = "" if left and right else "x"
    return ("" if left else " ") + word + ("" if right else " ")


def texts(command, tool):
    """The command's pieces: each command substitution on its own, then the
    rest with each substitution replaced by a word; and whether substitutions
    are nested past MAX_PASSES."""
    # Each shell's own line continuation: Bash joins `\` + LF with nothing
    # between, PowerShell reads a backtick before a line end as a space. A
    # backtick ending a Bash line and a `\` ending a PowerShell path stay.
    s = CONTINUATION[tool].sub(" " if tool == "PowerShell" else "", command)
    if tool != "PowerShell":
        s = neutral_cases(ANSI_QUOTE.sub(ansi_decode, s))
    else:
        s = POWERSHELL_CHAR.sub(lambda m: chr(min(int(m.group(1), 16), 0x10FFFF)), s)
    pieces = []
    if tool != "PowerShell":
        pieces += BACKTICK_GROUP.findall(s)
        s = BACKTICK_GROUP.sub(stand_in, s)
    for _ in range(MAX_PASSES):
        out, last = [], 0
        for match in INNERMOST[tool].finditer(s):
            inner = next(g for g in match.groups() if g is not None)
            literal = tool == "PowerShell" and LITERAL_GROUP.fullmatch(inner) is not None
            # A literal group stays in the text, so it is not read again here.
            if not literal:
                pieces.append(inner)
            out += [s[last:match.start()], stand_in(match, literal)]
            last = match.end()
        if not out:
            break
        out.append(s[last:])
        s = "".join(out)
    pieces.append(s)
    return pieces, INNERMOST[tool].search(s) is not None


def mask_quoted(text, tool):
    """The text with `;`, `|` and `&` inside quotes turned into spaces, so a
    quoted value (`-C "C:/R&D"`) stays in its statement. Only a quote that
    closes on its own line counts, so neither an apostrophe in a heredoc
    body or comment nor the closing quote of a string that spans lines can
    join statements. An escaped character outside quotes (`\\;`, `` `; ``,
    `\\"`) is text: it neither splits a statement nor opens a quote.

    Each character is read once: a quote with no close on its line means no
    later quote of that kind on the line closes either, so those are passed
    over instead of each searching to the end of the line again."""
    out, pos, unclosed = [], 0, set()
    while True:
        found = QUOTE_OR_LINE[tool].search(text, pos)
        if not found:
            break
        mark, at = found.group(0), found.start()
        if len(mark) == 2:
            out += [text[pos:at], mark[0] + QUOTED_SEPARATORS[tool].sub(" ", mark[1])]
            pos = found.end()
            continue
        if mark == "\n":
            unclosed.clear()
        elif mark not in unclosed:
            quoted = QUOTED[tool][mark].match(text, at)
            if quoted:
                out += [text[pos:at], QUOTED_SEPARATORS[tool].sub(" ", quoted.group(0))]
                pos = quoted.end()
                continue
            unclosed.add(mark)
        out.append(text[pos:at + 1])
        pos = at + 1
    out.append(text[pos:])
    return "".join(out)


def unquote(text, backslash):
    """The text without quote characters, backticks and `$` before a quote;
    a backslash is dropped (an escape) or read as a path separator."""
    text = re.sub(r"\$(?=[\"'])", "", text)
    text = re.sub("[\"'`\u2018\u2019\u201c\u201d]", "", text)
    return text.replace("\\", "/" if backslash == "path" else "")


def name(word):
    """The program a word names: its last path part, lowercased, without
    `.exe`."""
    return re.sub(r"\.exe$", "", word.strip(EDGE).split("/")[-1].lower())


def forces(word):
    """Whether one push argument forces: `--force`, a `--mirror` prefix, or a
    short-option bundle with `f` in it (`-qf`, `-4f`)."""
    if word.startswith("--"):
        return LONG_FORCE.fullmatch(word) is not None
    return "f" in word and SHORT_OPTIONS.fullmatch(word) is not None


def force_in(words):
    """Why the words of one statement force-push, or None. After a `git`
    word, a later push word starts the push, whatever sits between them: an
    option value split at its spaces (`-C "/c/My Repo"`) or a substitution's
    stand-in word. So does a one-off alias for push (`-c alias.p='push -f'
    p`), whose arguments follow its name. A word that is exactly a git
    subcommand in OTHER_SUBCOMMANDS, and is not the value of a git option,
    ends the search."""
    git, pushing, forcing, value = False, False, None, False
    for raw in words:
        word = raw.strip(EDGE)
        if pushing:
            if forces(word):
                return f"`{word}`"
            if word.startswith("+"):
                return f"`{word}` (a leading + forces that ref)"
            continue
        if value:
            value = False
            if FORCING_CONFIG.fullmatch(word):
                forcing = f"`-c {word}`"
            elif PUSH_ALIAS.fullmatch(word):
                pushing = True
            continue
        program = name(word)
        if program in PUSH_PROGRAMS:
            pushing = True
        elif program == "git":
            git = True
        elif not git:
            continue
        elif word in GIT_VALUE_OPTIONS:
            value = True
        elif FORCING_CONFIG.fullmatch(word):
            forcing = f"`-c {word}`"
        elif program in PUSH_SUBCOMMANDS or PUSH_ALIAS.fullmatch(word):
            if forcing:
                return forcing
            pushing = True
        elif word in OTHER_SUBCOMMANDS:
            # Another git command: its arguments are its own (`git commit -m
            # "push -f later"`).
            git, forcing = False, None
    return None


def redirect_gone(match):
    """What a redirect leaves: nothing, or its target when that names git, as
    in `bash <<< "git push -qf"`, which feeds the text to a shell."""
    target = match.group(1)
    return f" {target} " if name(target) == "git" or name(target) in PUSH_PROGRAMS else " "


def check(command, tool):
    """Why a command's text force-pushes, or None."""
    if len(command) > MAX_COMMAND:
        return None
    if tool == "Bash" and "\r" in command:
        # Git Bash drops every CR before reading, so `\` + CR + LF continues a
        # line there; Bash elsewhere keeps the CR. Either reading can block.
        return check_bash(command) or check_bash(command.replace("\r", ""))
    return check_bash(command) if tool == "Bash" else check_reading(command, tool)


def check_bash(command):
    """Why a Bash command's text force-pushes, or None."""
    tool = "Bash"
    if "\\\n" in command:
        # Bash does not continue a comment (`# C:\work\repo\`), a single-quoted
        # string or a quoted heredoc body, and telling those apart means
        # parsing Bash. Such a command is read whole instead, once with each
        # `\` + LF joined and once with it kept as a line end, each also as one
        # statement: a push anywhere in it with a force anywhere after blocks.
        for reading in (command, command.replace("\\\n", " \n")):
            reason = check_reading(reading, tool, whole=True)
            if reason:
                return reason
        return None
    return check_reading(command, tool)


def check_reading(command, tool, whole=False):
    """Why one reading of a command's text force-pushes, or None."""
    pieces, deep = texts(command, tool)
    for piece in pieces:
        masked = mask_quoted(piece, tool)
        for backslash in ("escape", "path"):
            # Redirects go once quotes are gone, so `git>/dev/null push` and
            # `push&>/dev/null` read as `git push`.
            text = REDIRECT.sub(redirect_gone, unquote(masked, backslash))
            # Substitutions nested past MAX_PASSES may hide separators, so such
            # a command is also read as one statement.
            # Read as one statement, the separators become spaces so a word
            # glued to one (`-f;`, `-qf|tail`) stays a word.
            whole_text = [STATEMENT_END[tool].sub(" ", text)] if deep or whole else []
            for statement in STATEMENT_END[tool].split(text) + whole_text:
                reason = force_in([w for w in WORD_SPLIT.split(statement) if w])
                if reason:
                    return reason
    return None


def main():
    try:
        # Claude Code writes UTF-8. Decode it as UTF-8 instead of the platform's
        # default encoding.
        data = json.loads(sys.stdin.buffer.read().decode("utf-8", "replace"))
    except ValueError:
        return 0
    tool = data.get("tool_name") if isinstance(data, dict) else None
    if tool not in ("Bash", "PowerShell"):
        return 0
    tool_input = data.get("tool_input")
    command = tool_input.get("command") if isinstance(tool_input, dict) else None
    if not isinstance(command, str):
        return 0
    # An error in the check exits 1, which the hook entry's onFailure turns into a refusal.
    reason = check(command, tool)
    if reason:
        print(f"Blocked a force push: {reason}. Use `--force-with-lease` instead, which refuses "
              "to overwrite commits you have not fetched. If the command only mentions a force "
              "push (a message, a script, a search), put that text in a file and pass the file. "
              "If it has a `\\` ending a line, put it on one line or run the push as its own "
              "command.",
              file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

#!/bin/sh
# Starts one of this repo's guard hooks: sh run-hook.sh <name>
# Claude Code pipes the tool call to stdin as JSON; the hook reads it there.
#
# The tool call goes ahead on purpose (exit 0) when:
# - ~/.claude/hooks/<name>.py exists and ~/.claude/settings.json names it
#   outside a permission rule, so the user's own copy runs and the check
#   never runs twice (a registration whose file is gone does not count);
# - no Python 3.8+ outside a virtual environment is on PATH;
# - this folder holds no hook file <name>.py.
#
# A hook that starts and then crashes, times out or exits with a code other
# than 0 or 2 is not handled here: the settings entry sets "onFailure":
# "block", so Claude Code blocks the tool call.
#
# A committed file cannot name the interpreter by absolute path, so this
# looks for one. A virtual environment's interpreter is refused because it
# can belong to the project. Python runs with -I, so the project's own
# modules cannot replace the ones the hook imports.

name=$1
hook="${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/.claude/hooks/$name.py"

settings="$HOME/.claude/settings.json"
# Permission entries look like "Bash(...)": a mention inside one is no
# registration. A line is dropped when the name sits inside such a string
# anywhere on it (compact arrays, minified files), so a line holding both a
# registration and a permission counts as neither and the hook runs twice,
# the safe side.
path="hooks[/\\\\]+$name\\.py"
if [ -f "$HOME/.claude/hooks/$name.py" ] && [ -f "$settings" ] &&
  grep -E "$path" "$settings" | grep -Evq "\"[A-Za-z]+\\(([^\"\\\\]|\\\\.)*$path"; then
  exit 0
fi

[ -f "$hook" ] || exit 0

for py in python3 python py; do
  if "$py" -I -c 'import sys; sys.exit(sys.version_info < (3, 8) or sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    exec "$py" -I -c 'import runpy, sys; runpy.run_path(sys.argv[1], run_name="__main__")' "$hook"
  fi
done

echo "Guard hook $name did not run: no Python 3.8+ found outside a virtual environment." >&2
exit 0

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PreToolUse guard: refuse the shell patterns a session was told to stop using.

Each rule in RULES names a pattern that keeps failing, why, and what to use
instead. A correction of the kind "never use X, use Y" lands here as a new rule,
so the session cannot drift back to X: a note in memory alone does not hold.

Rules other than the inline-script one read the command with quoted strings
and PowerShell here-string bodies taken out, and a bash command only as far as
its first here-document, so a commit message or a PR body that only mentions a
pattern passes. The inline-script rule reads a bash command's first
here-document, only when its `<<` stands outside quotes, and PowerShell
here-strings, and refuses one only where an interpreter reads its script from
standard input (`python -`, `cat <<EOF | node`): fed to a script file, the text
is data. It also reads the script of a `python -c` or `node -e` call that
stands outside quotes and comments. Where the reading is unsure (a quote that
never closes, a double-quoted string holding `$(`, a `<<` inside one), the
text is left unread: a missed pattern costs less than a refused command. It is
a safety net for the ordinary spelling, not a sandbox against a command built
to slip past it.

Each rule carries its mode. An `enforce` rule refuses the command. An `observe`
rule only appends what it would have refused to the user's Bindwright folder
(OBSERVED_LOG), which `/bindwright:doctor` reports, so a false refusal shows up
before anyone is stopped. A new rule ships as `observe` and moves to `enforce`
in a later release once its log shows none. The mode lives here, never in a
file a session could write, so nothing at run time relaxes a rule.

Exit contract: JSON permissionDecision=deny on stdout, exit 0. Silent exit 0
otherwise, and for any input it cannot read.
"""
import bisect
import json
import os
import re
import sys
import time

INTERPRETER = r"(?:python3?|py|node|deno|bun|perl|ruby|php|bash|sh|zsh|pwsh|powershell)(?:\.exe)?"
PROGRAM = re.compile(r"(?:.*[/\\])?" + INTERPRETER, re.I)
# The short-option letters that hand each interpreter its script some other way (`python -Ic`,
# `perl -ne`, `php -r`), so standard input is data; short letters are never abbreviated.
SCRIPT_LETTERS = {"python": "cm", "py": "cm", "node": "ep", "bun": "e", "perl": "eE", "ruby": "e",
                  "php": "rf", "bash": "c", "sh": "c", "zsh": "c"}
SCRIPT_LONG = {"--eval", "--print", "--command", "--file"}
POWERSHELL_SCRIPT = {"-c", "-command", "-f", "-file", "-e", "-ec", "-encodedcommand"}
SHELLS = ("bash", "sh", "zsh")
REDIRECTION = re.compile(r"\d*(?:&>|[<>]&?)")
# A here-document opener, its word quoted (`<<'EOF'`, `<<"EOF"`), escaped (`<<\EOF`) or bare.
HEREDOC = re.compile(r"<<(-?)[ \t]*\\?(['\"]?)([A-Za-z_][\w-]*)\2")
# A `<<` that is not part of a here-string (`<<<`); `without_arithmetic` blanks arithmetic, where a
# `<<` opens nothing.
HEREDOC_OPERATOR = re.compile(r"(?<!<)<<(?!<)")
# A PowerShell here-string: `@'` or `@"` and any blanks to the end of the line, the body (none when
# the closing line comes next), then the first line that starts with the same quote and `@`.
HERE_STRING_PARTS = r"@({quotes})[ \t]*\r?\n(?:(.*?)\r?\n)??\1@"
HERE_STRING = re.compile(HERE_STRING_PARTS.format(quotes="['\"]") + r"([^\n]*)", re.S)
# The separators between the commands of one line, a lone `&` (run in the background) among them
# but not a redirection (`2>&1`, `&>f`) or `|&`; a pipe joins two parts of one command.
LIST_SEPARATOR = re.compile(r"&&|\|\||;|(?<![>&|])&(?![>&])")

INLINE = re.compile(r"(?:^|[\s;&|(])(?:python3?|py)(?:\.exe)?(?:[ \t]+-\w+)*[ \t]+-c[ \t]+(['\"])(.*?)\1"

INLINE_CALL = re.compile(r"(?:^|[\s;&|(])(?:(?:python3?|py)(?:\.exe)?(?:[ \t]+-\w+)*[ \t]+-c"

# Comments, quoted strings and escapes as each shell reads them, in one pass across lines, so
# whichever starts first wins: a `#` that starts a word outside quotes comments out the rest of
# its line, and a quote character in a comment opens nothing. Bash escapes with a backslash,
# PowerShell with a backtick and by doubling the quote, and a PowerShell backslash is plain text
# (`"C:\"`). A PowerShell block comment runs from `<#` to the first `#>`. Bash's `$'...'` ends
# only at an unescaped quote. A quote or block comment that never closes, and a double-quoted
# string holding `$(`, whose own quotes nest, run to the end of the command. A PowerShell
# here-string (`@'` to a line starting `'@`) is one more quoted string in the same scan, so one
# inside a message or a comment is part of that text.
COMMENT = r"(?:^|(?<=[\s;&|(]))#[^\n]*"
QUOTED = {"bash": re.compile(COMMENT + r"|\\.|\$'(?:[^'\\]|\\.)*(?:'|\Z)|'[^']*(?:'|\Z)"
                             r"|\"(?:[^\"\\$]|\\.|\$(?!\())*\$\(.*|\"(?:[^\"\\]|\\.)*(?:\"|\Z)", re.S)}
POWERSHELL_QUOTED = (r"<#.*?(?:#>|\Z)|" + COMMENT + r"|`.|'(?:[^']|'')*(?:'|\Z)"
                     r"|\"(?:[^\"`$]|`.|\"\"|\$(?!\())*\$\(.*|\"(?:[^\"`]|`.|\"\")*(?:\"|\Z)")
# The PowerShell scan for each set of quotes whose here-strings may still close. An opener with
# no closing line after it never matches, and trying one reads to the end of the command, so the
# scan leaves those out: many of them would take time that grows with the command's length squared.
POWERSHELL_SCANS = {quotes: re.compile((HERE_STRING_PARTS.format(quotes="[%s]" % quotes) + "|" if quotes else "")
                                       + POWERSHELL_QUOTED, re.S) for quotes in ("'\"", "'", "\"", "")}

POWERSHELL_QUOTE_START = re.compile(r"[@<#`'\"]")

GIT_BASH = os.name == "nt"

JQ = re.compile(r"(?:^|(?<=[\s;&|(]))jq(?:\.exe)?(?=\s|$)")

WRITE_THE_FILE = "its backslashes get eaten. Write the script with the Write tool, then run the file."


def blanked(match):
    """The matched text as spaces, line ends kept, so the positions around it stay put."""
    return re.sub(r"[^\n]", " ", match.group())


def as_quote(match):
    """A quoted string as its opening quote and spaces, a comment or an escape as spaces, line
    ends kept, so the text keeps its length, a call's position in it matches the original's, and
    the quote a script starts with stays where it is, whatever follows it."""
    spaces = blanked(match)
    if match.group()[:1] in "'\"":
        return match.group()[0] + spaces[1:]
    return spaces


def without_arithmetic(text):
    """The text with each `((...))` and `$((...))` blanked, where a `<<` opens nothing: an opener
    closes at the first `)` after it when a second `)` follows. That `)` is found once and kept for
    every opener before it, since searching from each opener takes time that grows with the square
    of a long run of `(`."""
    parts, at, look, close = [], 0, 0, -1
    while True:
        opener = text.find("((", look)
        if opener == -1:
            break
        if close < opener + 2:
            close = text.find(")", opener + 2)
            if close == -1:
                break
        start = opener - 1 if opener > at and text[opener - 1] == "$" else opener
        if text.startswith(")", close + 1):
            parts += [text[at:start], re.sub(r"[^\n]", " ", text[start:close + 2])]
            at = look = close + 2
        else:
            look = opener + 1
    return "".join(parts) + text[at:]


def as_word(match):
    """A quoted string as one placeholder word the length of the original, line ends kept, so a
    quoted argument (`python3 "$HOOK"`) still counts as a word."""
    return re.sub(r"^[^\n]", "Q", blanked(match))


def first_opener(text):
    """(line number, match) of the first line that may open a here-document, quoted or not, or
    None: a `<<` that is not part of a here-string (`<<<`) followed by a word."""
    for number, line in enumerate(text.split("\n")):
        for operator in HEREDOC_OPERATOR.finditer(line):
            match = HEREDOC.match(line, operator.start())
            if match:
                return number, match
    return None


def heredoc(text):
    """(receivers, body) of a bash command's first here-document, or None when it has none or its
    `<<` stands inside quotes, a comment or arithmetic, where the reading is unsure
    (`"$(cat <<'EOF'`). The receivers are the commands of its pipeline from the one the `<<` feeds
    on (`cat <<EOF | python3`), with quoted strings blanked."""
    first = first_opener(text)
    if not first:
        return None
    number, match = first
    masked = without_arithmetic(QUOTED["bash"].sub(as_word, text)).split("\n")[number]
    if not HEREDOC_OPERATOR.match(masked, match.start()):
        return None
    before = LIST_SEPARATOR.split(masked[:match.start()])[-1].split("|")[-1]
    after = LIST_SEPARATOR.split(masked[match.end():])[0].split("|")
    body = []
    for line in text.split("\n")[number + 1:]:
        if ends_heredoc(line, match):
            break
        body.append(line)
    return [before + after[0]] + after[1:], "\n".join(body)


def ends_heredoc(line, match):
    """Whether a line is the terminator of the here-document `match` opened."""
    line = line.rstrip("\r")
    return (line.lstrip("\t") if match.group(1) else line) == match.group(3)


def program_words(command):
    """A command's words without the `NAME=value` assignments before or among them."""
    return [word for word in command.split() if not re.fullmatch(r"\w+=\S*", word)]


def interpreter_name(word):
    """`python3.exe` and `/usr/bin/python3` as `python`: the key the option tables use."""
    return re.sub(r"\d+$", "", re.sub(r"(?i)\.exe$", "", re.split(r"[/\\]", word)[-1]).lower())


def gives_script(word, name):
    """Whether an option hands the interpreter its script itself (`-c`, `-ne`, `--eval=...`)."""
    if word.startswith("--"):
        return word.split("=", 1)[0].lower() in SCRIPT_LONG
    if name in ("pwsh", "powershell"):
        return word.lower() in POWERSHELL_SCRIPT
    return any(letter in word[1:] for letter in SCRIPT_LETTERS.get(name, ""))


def reads_script(command):
    """Whether this command is an interpreter that reads its script from standard input: nothing
    but options after it (`python`, `node`), `-`, or `-s` for a shell. A script file, a module or
    an inline script (`python3 x.py`, `python -m pkg`, `perl -ne '...'`) reads standard input as
    data, and so does an option whose value is unknown (`python -W x`); a script option given `-`
    (`pwsh -Command -`) reads it from standard input after all."""
    words = program_words(command)
    if not words or not PROGRAM.fullmatch(words[0]):
        return False
    name = interpreter_name(words[0])
    rest, k = words[1:], 0
    while k < len(rest):
        word = rest[k]
        if REDIRECTION.match(word):
            k += 2 if REDIRECTION.fullmatch(word) else 1  # a bare `>` names its target next
            continue
        if word == "-":
            return True
        if not word.startswith("-"):
            return False
        if gives_script(word, name):
            return rest[k + 1:k + 2] == ["-"]
        if name in SHELLS and re.fullmatch(r"-[a-z]*s[a-z]*", word):
            return True
        k += 1
    return True


def first_interpreter_reads(commands):
    """Whether the first interpreter among a pipeline's commands reads its script from standard
    input. Commands before it (`cat`, `sed`) pass the text on; once an interpreter has read it,
    later ones get only its output (`python3 gen.py <<EOF | sh`)."""
    for command in commands:
        words = program_words(command)
        if words and PROGRAM.fullmatch(words[0]):
            return reads_script(command)
    return False


def piped_to(rest_of_line):
    """The commands a PowerShell here-string is piped into: the pipeline after its closing line."""
    return re.split(r";|&&|\|\|", rest_of_line)[0].split("|")[1:]


def inline_script(text, shell):
    """Whether an interpreter is handed a script holding a backslash."""
    found = heredoc(text) if shell == "bash" else None
    if found and "\\" in found[1] and first_interpreter_reads(found[0]):
        return True
    if shell == "powershell" and any("\\" in (here.group(2) or "")
                                     and first_interpreter_reads(piped_to(here.group(3)))
                                     for here in here_strings(text)):
        return True
    # A `python -c '...'` a message only mentions leaves no call where its quotes are taken out.
    masked, end = masked_calls(text, shell)
    return any("\\" in (m.group(2) or m.group(4) or "") and m.start() < end and INLINE_CALL.match(masked, m.start())
               for m in INLINE.finditer(text))


def here_strings(text):
    """The PowerShell here-strings that stand outside quotes and comments, with the rest of the
    line each one ends on: the quote scan meets them before anything that would hold them."""
    return [HERE_STRING.match(text, m.start()) for m in quoted(text, "powershell") if m.group().startswith("@")]


def quoted(text, shell):
    """The quoted strings, comments and escapes the shell's scan finds, in order. A PowerShell
    here-string opener is tried only while a line that may close it follows."""
    if shell == "bash":
        return list(QUOTED["bash"].finditer(text))
    closes = {quote: text.rfind("\n" + quote + "@") for quote in "'\""}
    found, at = [], 0
    while True:
        start = POWERSHELL_QUOTE_START.search(text, at)
        if not start:
            return found
        quotes = "".join(quote for quote in "'\"" if closes[quote] > start.start())
        match = POWERSHELL_SCANS[quotes].match(text, start.start())
        if match:
            found.append(match)
        at = match.end() if match else start.start() + 1


def masked(text, shell, replace):
    """The command with each match of the shell's scan replaced by `replace`, a text or a
    function of the match, as `re.sub` takes it."""
    parts, at = [], 0
    for match in quoted(text, shell):
        parts += [text[at:match.start()], replace(match) if callable(replace) else replace]
        at = match.end()
    return "".join(parts + [text[at:]])


def masked_calls(text, shell):
    """(the command with quoted strings, comments and PowerShell here-strings masked to the same
    length, where a call may stand): a bash command only up to the end of the first line that may
    open a here-document, as in `bare`."""
    end = len(text)
    if shell == "bash":
        first = first_opener(text)
        if first:
            end = len("\n".join(text.split("\n")[:first[0] + 1]))
    return masked(text, shell, as_quote), end


def bare(text, shell):
    """The command with quoted strings taken out, and PowerShell here-string bodies; a bash
    command only up to the end of the first line that may open a here-document, quoted or not
    (`"$(cat <<'EOF'`), since reading too little only misses a pattern."""
    if shell == "bash":
        first = first_opener(text)
        if first:
            text = "\n".join(text.split("\n")[:first[0] + 1])
    return masked(text, shell, "''")


class Followed:
    """A search for `head`, then any characters but `stops`, then `rest`: the same answer as one
    pattern joining them, in time linear in the text. Every head whose run ends at the same stop
    finds `rest` only where the head ending first does, so `rest` is tried once per stop, where
    the joined pattern tries it once per head and a line repeating the head takes time that grows
    with its length squared. `skip_line` names text whose line a head may not start on."""

    def __init__(self, head, stops, rest, flags=re.I, skip_line=()):
        self.head = re.compile(head, flags)
        self.stop = re.compile("[%s]" % stops)
        self.tail = re.compile("[^%s]*%s" % (stops, rest), flags)
        self.skip_line = skip_line

    def skips(self, text, newlines, line):
        begin = newlines[line - 1] + 1 if line else 0
        end = newlines[line] if line < len(newlines) else len(text)
        return any(word in text[begin:end] for word in self.skip_line)

    def search(self, text):
        stops = [match.start() for match in self.stop.finditer(text)]
        newlines = [match.start() for match in re.finditer("\n", text)] if self.skip_line else []
        skipped, tried = {}, set()
        for head in self.head.finditer(text):
            run_end = bisect.bisect_left(stops, head.end())
            if run_end in tried:
                continue
            if self.skip_line:
                line = bisect.bisect_left(newlines, head.start())
                if line not in skipped:
                    skipped[line] = self.skips(text, newlines, line)
                if skipped[line]:
                    continue
            tried.add(run_end)
            if self.tail.match(text, head.end()):
                return True
        return False


def both(*patterns):
    """A test that holds when every pattern (a regex, or a `Followed`) is found in the bare command."""
    compiled = [p if isinstance(p, Followed) else re.compile(p, re.I) for p in patterns]
    return lambda text, shell: all(p.search(bare(text, shell)) for p in compiled)


def cased(pattern):
    """Like `both`, for one test whose letter case carries meaning (`-b` is not `-B`)."""
    compiled = pattern if isinstance(pattern, Followed) else re.compile(pattern)
    return lambda text, shell: bool(compiled.search(bare(text, shell)))


# `origin/develop:.claude/x`: a git object path that starts with a dot.
REV_DOT_PATH = Followed(r"\bgit\s+(?:show|cat-file|ls-tree|diff)\b", r"\n|;&", r"\s[\w./@~^-]+:\.[^/\s.]")

ENFORCE = "enforce"
OBSERVE = "observe"
OBSERVED_LOG = os.path.join(os.path.expanduser("~"), ".bindwright", "tool-rules", "observed.jsonl")
# Past this many bytes the log moves to a single `.old` copy and starts over, so it never grows unbounded.
OBSERVED_LOG_LIMIT = 256 * 1024
# A run of 24 or more letters, digits and _-+/= holding a digit reads as a token or key (base64 included):
# the log keeps a placeholder. The digit is checked on each run found, since a lookahead for it
# makes a long run take time that grows with its length squared.
TOKEN_RUN = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9_\-+/=]{24,}")


def without_tokens(text):
    return TOKEN_RUN.sub(lambda run: "<token>" if re.search(r"\d", run.group()) else run.group(), text)

RULES = [
    ("an inline script holding a backslash", inline_script, WRITE_THE_FILE, ENFORCE),
    ("`gh run watch`", both(r"\bgh\s+run\s+watch\b"),
     "it blocks the session. ci-watch (or a bounded watcher, token-efficiency.md) watches checks.", ENFORCE),
    ("the size check chained with a commit or push",
     both(r"(?:^|(?<=[\s;&|(]))(?:python3?|py)(?:\.exe)?\s+(?:-\S+\s+)*\S*size_check\.py",
          r"\bgit\s+(?:commit|push)\b"),
     "the commit runs past its breaches. Run size_check.py in its own call first.", ENFORCE),
    ("`git push` and `gh pr create` in one command", both(r"\bgit\s+push\b", r"\bgh\s+pr\s+create\b"),
     "the chain gets refused. Push, then open the PR in a separate call.", ENFORCE),
    ("`git checkout <rev> -- <path>`", both(r"\bgit\s+checkout\s+(?!-)\S+\s+--\s+\S"),
     "it overwrites and stages those files. Peek with `git show <rev>:./<path>`; restore with `git restore`.",
     ENFORCE),
    ("`gh pr merge --admin`", both(Followed(r"\bgh\s+pr\s+merge\b", r"\n", r"\s--admin\b")),
     "it skips the required checks. Fix what blocks the merge.", ENFORCE),
    ("`<rev>:.<path>` in Git Bash",
     lambda text, shell: GIT_BASH and shell == "bash" and REV_DOT_PATH.search(bare(text, shell)),
     "Git Bash rewrites it, so the file looks missing. Write `<rev>:./<path>` from the repo root.", ENFORCE),
    ("`gh run rerun --failed` or `--job`",
     both(Followed(r"\bgh\s+run\s+rerun\b", r"\n|;&", r"\s(?:--failed|--job|-j)\b")),
     "a re-run of only some jobs can leave a required check stuck. Re-run the whole run, or push again.", OBSERVE),
    ("an interactive git command (`-i`, `-p`)",
     # `git stash show -p` only prints, and a rebase given a scripted editor never waits for keys.
     cased(Followed(r"\bgit\s+(?:rebase|add|checkout|reset|stash(?!\s+(?:show|list)\b)|restore|clean)\b",
                    r"\n|;&", r"\s(?:-i|--interactive|-p|--patch)\b", flags=0,
                    skip_line=("GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=", "sequence.editor="))),
     "it waits for an editor or keys a tool call cannot give. Use the form that takes its input in the command.",
     OBSERVE),
    ("an inline body for `gh pr` or `gh issue`",
     cased(Followed(r"\bgh\s+(?:pr|issue)\s+(?:create|comment|edit|review)\b", r"\n|;&",
                    r"\s(?:--body|-b)(?:[=\s]|$)", flags=0)),
     "the shell can cut or change the text. Write the body to a file and pass `--body-file`.", OBSERVE),
    ("a scratch file in a fixed folder (`/tmp`, `C:/tmp`)",
     # Claude Code's own session scratchpad lives under /tmp/claude-<id>/ on Linux.
     both(r"(?:^|(?<=[\s=>]))(?:/tmp|[a-z]:[\\/]tmp)(?![\w.-]|/claude-\d+/)"),
     "other sessions share it, and nothing cleans it up. Use the session's scratchpad instead.", OBSERVE),
    ("`jq` in Git Bash", lambda text, shell: GIT_BASH and shell == "bash" and JQ.search(bare(text, shell)),
     "Git Bash has no `jq`. Filter with the `--jq` option of `gh`, or with Python.", OBSERVE),

def observe(name, text, shell):
    """Append one would-be refusal to OBSERVED_LOG; a log that cannot be written is skipped."""
    entry = {"time": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z"), "rule": name, "shell": shell,
             "command": without_tokens(text)[:500]}
    try:
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(OBSERVED_LOG), exist_ok=True)
        if os.path.exists(OBSERVED_LOG) and os.path.getsize(OBSERVED_LOG) > OBSERVED_LOG_LIMIT:
            os.replace(OBSERVED_LOG, OBSERVED_LOG + ".old")
        with open(OBSERVED_LOG, "a", encoding="utf-8") as log:
            log.write(json.dumps(entry) + "\n")
    except OSError:
        pass


def refusal(text, shell):
    """The first enforce rule the command breaks, as (name, why), or None.

    Observe rules it breaks before that one are logged."""
    for name, test, why, mode in RULES:
        if not test(text, shell):
            continue
        if mode == ENFORCE:
            return name, why
        observe(name, text, shell)
    return None


def deny(name, why):
    sys.stdout.write(json.dumps({"hookSpecificOutput": {
        "hookEventName": "PreToolUse", "permissionDecision": "deny",
        "permissionDecisionReason": f"BLOCKED (tool rule): {name}: {why}",
    }}))
    sys.exit(0)


def main():
    try:
        data = json.loads(sys.stdin.buffer.read().decode("utf-8-sig"))
        text = data["tool_input"]["command"]
    except Exception:
        sys.exit(0)
    if not isinstance(text, str):
        sys.exit(0)
    shell = "powershell" if data.get("tool_name") == "PowerShell" else "bash"
    refused = refusal(text, shell)
    if refused:
        deny(*refused)
    sys.exit(0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Clean code

A developer who just arrived opens any file and understands it at once, even with the comments stripped. Size limits live in `code-size.md` and dead code in `git.md`; this file covers the rest. Generated or vendored code is out of scope.

## The newcomer test

Before committing, read the change as someone who knows the product but none of its planning history. Every name says what the thing is, every function does the one job its name states, and a comment adds only what the code cannot show. If a sentence needs a codename, a date or a past measurement to make sense, it fails.

## Comments

- Say what the code does now and the constraint it cannot show: units, invariants, who owns a thread, a data format, why a value is this value. Never restate the line below.
- One line by default. A block comment is for a data format, a contract between systems or an algorithm that is not obvious. A comment longer than the code it explains means the code or its name should change instead.
- No history: no "was", "used to", "previously", "replaces", "added for", dated measurements or the story of a bug hunt. The commit message, the PR and the docs hold that.
- A tuning value states the limit, not the session that found it: "past 16 rebuilds a frame the render thread stalls", not "twenty measured a 100 ms stall on Tuesday". A measurement `code-size.md` asks for is stated the same way, as the limit it shows.
- A comment changes with its code. A comment that no longer matches the code is a bug.
- Public surface gets a doc comment in the language's own form. Private helpers with clear names need none.

## Names

- Spell names out where a full word fits: `chunk_coord`, not `cc`. Domain-standard short forms stay: `x`, `y`, `i`, `j`, `dx`, and the symbols of a formula its header defines.
- No planning codes in code: milestone or slice tags, issue or PR numbers, dates that tag when work happened, and review-round references never appear in comments, identifiers or strings. One exception: a skipped test or a temporary workaround links the issue that tracks its removal, or names its title where a project check bans issue numbers in code. Name a system by what it does. Real file paths are fine; they are pointers, not tags.
- Booleans read as questions (`is_loaded`, `has_mesh`), functions as verbs (`build_mesh`), and one concept keeps one name across files.

## Structure

- One job per function and per class. A class whose methods split into separate groups becomes helpers behind the same surface.
- No copies. The second copy of a helper is the moment to share it; a parameter or a generic replaces two near-identical bodies. A mutant check in a test (`testing.md`) is a deliberate copy, not a duplicate.
- Straight-line logic: no set-then-undo (turn a flag on, write through it, turn it off); write the end state directly. Prefer early returns to deep nesting.
- Match the file: follow the surrounding code's naming, comment density and idiom.

Review blocks a breach. `docs/comment-audit.md` holds the method for trimming the comments of existing code to this rule.

# Code size

Soft limit: the reviewer mentions it, nothing is owed. Hard limit: a blocking finding unless the code falls under an exception below. Lines are physical lines including blanks and comments; a function counts from its signature to its closing brace.

## Every language

| Construct | Soft | Hard |
|---|---|---|
| Nesting depth | 4 | 6 |
| Parameters | 5 | 8 |
| Cyclomatic complexity per function | 15 | 25 |
| Inline lambda or closure | 15 lines | 40 lines |

## Per language

Keep the rows for this project's languages and delete the rest.

| Language | File | Function | Line length |
|---|---|---|---|
| C / C++ | 800 (.h 400) / 1 500 (.h 800) | 60 / 150 | 100 / 120 |
| C# / Java / Kotlin | 600 / 1 200 | 50 / 100 | 100 / 120 |
| Dart | 600 / 1 200 (build method 80 / 150) | 50 / 100 | 80 / 120 |
| GDScript | 600 / 1 200 | 40 / 80 | 100 / 120 |
| Go | 800 / 1 500 | 60 / 120 | 100 / 120 |
| JavaScript / TypeScript | 400 / 800 | 50 / 100 | 100 / 120 |
| Python | 500 / 1 000 | 50 / 100 | 100 / 120 |
| Rust | 800 / 1 500 | 60 / 120 | 100 / 120 |
| Other | 600 / 1 200 | 50 / 100 | 100 / 120 |

Values are soft / hard. Test files may run 1.5 times the file limit.

## Exceptions

1. Generated or vendored code: out of scope.
2. Declarative data (tables, schemas, translation files): no file limit.
3. Test batteries of many small cases: file limit only.
4. A hot loop kept in one function for measured performance: allowed past soft with a comment stating the measurement. Never past hard.

## Working the rule

New code meets the table from its first commit. A new file or function that would pass the hard limit is designed smaller before it lands: extract functions, split the file, flatten nesting with early returns. Existing code over the limit shrinks when it is next substantially changed, not in drive-by edits.

## The check

`.github/scripts/size_check.py` measures the mechanical rows of these tables on every PR (`.github/workflows/size-check.yml`): file and line length, and each function's length, complexity and parameters. Breaches the project had when the check was set up are recorded in `.github/size-check/baseline.txt` and may only shrink; any new hard breach fails the PR. Delete a baseline line once its code complies; the check fails until you do, so a leftover line cannot excuse the next breach. A breach under one of the exceptions above goes in `.github/size-check/exceptions.txt` with its reason. `--report` lists every finding, soft ones included. Edit the tables here, not in the script: it reads them from this file.
