# Git rules

## Commits

One logical change per commit. Never mix a feature with a refactor, or a fix with config.

```
<type>(<scope>): <imperative description>
```

- 72 characters max. Imperative verb: `add`, `fix`, `remove`, `update`, `refactor`, `extract`.
- `scope` is the system or layer touched.
- Types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `docs`, `chore` (build, CI, tooling, deps), `data` (app data, configs, assets), `style` (formatting only).
- No AI-attribution lines anywhere: no co-author trailers, "generated with" footers or session links in commits, PR titles, PR bodies or comments. `.claude/settings.json` turns off the harness's own trailers, and the `no-ai-attribution` hook catches the ones written by hand.

---

## Branches (Gitflow)

| Branch | From | Merges into |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | | Production. Every release commit is tagged. |
| `develop` | | Integration. Base for all work. |
| `feature/<name>` | `develop` | `develop` |
| `release/<version>` | `develop` | `main`, then cascade to `develop` |
| `hotfix/<name>` | `main` | `main`, then cascade to `develop` |

- Kebab-case names: `feature/user-auth-flow`.
- Never push directly to `main` or `develop`.
- The GitHub default branch is `main`, so always pass `--base develop` to `gh pr create` for work PRs.

### Keep branches current

When the base branch advances, merge it into your open branches before continuing (`git fetch origin`, then `git merge origin/develop` on the work branch, then push). Never rewrite a branch someone else has pulled.

### Scope

A branch changes one concern. A tangential bug gets its own branch. Before coding, list the directories the work will touch; anything outside the branch's scope becomes a prerequisite branch and PR that merges first.

### Check the branch before the first edit

Run `git branch --show-current` before editing. Switch or branch first, then edit. If you notice you edited on the wrong branch, stop and say so instead of stashing and moving the work silently.

---

## Merging

- Every PR merges with a merge commit: `gh pr merge <pr> --merge --delete-branch`. Keep each commit buildable, and read history with `git log --first-parent`.
- Release PRs (`develop` into `main`) and cascade PRs (`main` into `develop`) always use `--merge`. Squashing them makes the two branches diverge and turns the next release into a conflict.
- After merging: `--delete-branch` removes the remote branch, but the local one only when it is checked out. Run `git branch -D <name>` if it remains, then confirm with `git branch`.
- Then, when Bindwright's helper is installed (`~/.bindwright/helper/node_modules/bindwright`, which setup installs), run `node "$HOME/.bindwright/helper/node_modules/bindwright/hooks/counts.mjs" send <repo root>` in the background. It sends nothing unless this computer turned on the anonymous review counts, and at most once in 24 hours, so a merge never waits on it.
- Re-run a failed CI workflow as a whole (or push again). Re-running only the failed job can leave a required check stuck.

### Cascade after every merge into `main`

GitHub does not copy `main` back into `develop`. After a hotfix or release merges:

```bash
git fetch origin
git checkout -b chore/cascade-<name> origin/develop
git merge --no-ff origin/main -m "chore: cascade <name> into develop"
git push -u origin chore/cascade-<name>
gh pr create --base develop --title "chore: cascade <name> into develop" --body-file <file>
```

The hotfix or release is done only when the cascade PR is merged and its branch deleted.

### Workflow file changes

Review workflows triggered by comments or schedules run the copy on the GitHub default branch, and the review app refuses its token to a run whose copy of the review workflow differs from that copy, so its review is never posted.
Because `main` is the default branch, a change to `.github/workflows/` lands on `main` first as a `hotfix/<name>` PR, then cascades to `develop`. A workflow change made on a feature branch fails the review check.

---

## Pull requests

Write the body to a file and pass `--body-file <path>`. Inline bodies get truncated or mangled by the shell.

```
## What
<1-3 bullets>

## Why
<1-2 lines>

## Notes (optional)
<non-obvious decisions, performance impact, manual steps>
```

No empty sections and no generic testing checklist. The body carries what the diff cannot show.

Review tiers, the verdict rule and CI watching live in `review-tiers.md` and `token-efficiency.md`.

---

## Versioning

Size each release by what its users must do:

- **Major:** they must act, or something they use stops working: a command, option or API removed or renamed with no old name kept, a file or save format that old data cannot load, a raised minimum OS, runtime or tool version.
- **Minor:** new features, or changed defaults that keep everything working.
- **Patch:** fixes only.

When a release tool sets the version and the tag, feed it the way its configuration reads and never bump or tag by hand. Otherwise bump every file that carries the version together, and tag the release commit in the style the existing tags use. With a changelog, each change a user must act on goes under `### Breaking`. A project that does not version its releases skips this section.

`.github/scripts/version_check.py <version>` reads the commits since the last release and refuses a version smaller than they need, or a changelog section that does not match it. Run it before each `git tag <version>`, `gh release create <version>` and `gh pr create` from a `release/<version>` branch; where the guard hooks live in the repo, a hook runs it on those commands by itself. Pick the version and the sections it names; never tag around it.

## Dead code does not ship

Code with no remaining caller is deleted in the same PR that orphaned it. Check with the project's lint or dead-code tool, then judge the result: a symbol reached only through reflection, dependency injection, bindings or serialization is not dead. If a tool reports a false positive, record the exception where the tool reads it instead of silencing the tool.

## Definition of done

A feature is done when it works end to end in the running app, not when it compiles. CI green is necessary, not sufficient. When `.claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md` exists, run `/verify` before each commit of a change people can see or use.

# Review tiers

Every PR gets an AI review with a pass or block verdict, run by `.github/workflows/`. Local sessions never start the CI reviews themselves; the one local review is the workflow-only PR path in § PRs that edit the review workflow.

| Tier | Starts when | Model |
|---|---|---|
| Routine | Every PR with reviewable files (`claude-code-review.yml`) | `claude-fable-5-2` at low effort; backup `claude-opus-5-5` at high |
| Deep | A comment starting with `@claude review this PR` (`claude.yml`) | `claude-fable-5-2` at medium effort; backup `claude-opus-5-5` at high |

Both tiers report into one check, `Review gate`: it passes when the routine verdict is 🟢 and, once a deep review is asked for, the deep verdict is 🟢 too. That check, beside any other checks the project requires, is required on protected branches, and branch protection has no bypass actors; `.github/scripts/setup-review-gate.sh` sets this up (`--check` only reports what is missing). With a single maintainer, require zero approvals so the gate alone decides, since authors cannot approve their own PRs. With more people, also require one approval from someone other than the author. Docs-only and other non-reviewable diffs pass automatically in about 30 seconds.

The gate's settings live in `.github/review-gate.yml` (models, runner, the project's own pre-screen checks, trigger paths and always-reviewed paths), and the project's part of the review prompt lives in `.github/review-guide.md`. Both are read from the PR's base branch, so a PR cannot change the rules of its own review. Model pins change only after a side-by-side comparison of candidate models on the same saved PRs, never just because a newer model exists.

## The verdict rule (both tiers)

- 🟢 LGTM only when the review is fully clean: no caveats, no nits, no "non-blocking" findings.
- 🔴 Blocking when any real finding exists, however it is framed. "LGTM with caveats" is 🔴.
- Style preferences and speculative future-proofing are dropped, not listed as minor.

A 🟢 that carries findings lets them merge and come back later as the same review.

## Deep review triggers

The routine reviewer escalates automatically: it adds the `needs-deep-review` label and posts the `@claude review this PR` comment when the diff touches the gate's own files, the trigger paths and patterns in `.github/review-gate.yml` (`escalate.*`), or the list below. While that label is on the PR, every push gets a deep review, and the gate waits for its 🟢.

Escalate on risk, not size:

- Parsing, encoding or serialization logic
- Threading, locking, async coordination
- Schedulers, graph or DAG algorithms
- New public API surface
- Save or load formats, schema migrations
- Authentication, authorization, secrets, cryptography
- Anything that crosses a trust boundary (user input, network, plugins)

Skip escalation for docs, CI or settings tweaks, version bumps, mechanical refactors, test-only changes and one-line fixes. Fit the list to the project's risk: paths and added-line patterns go in `.github/review-gate.yml` (`escalate.paths`, `escalate.patterns`), changes that need judgment to spot go in `.github/review-guide.md` under "Also escalate when the diff includes". Keep this list in step with both.

## After a 🔴

Fix on the same PR branch and push; the review re-runs. Then search the codebase for the same mistake elsewhere and fix every copy in that commit, because the reviewer only sees the diff. When the same finding already came up on an earlier PR, add it to the checklist in `.github/review-guide.md` in the same PR: a trigger the diff shows, the check, and both PRs. A PR that must hold only its own files (§ PRs that edit the review workflow, § If the gate itself breaks) leaves the item to the next PR. Every later review then checks it whenever the trigger matches.

## What a finding blocks on

A finding belongs to the PR when the PR causes it: a regression from the base branch, or a break of what the PR says it does. A gap the base branch already has, or one the comparable community tool shares (for a workflow, the official action it pins), is not the PR's finding. It goes into a follow-up issue instead of the verdict. The review still covers the whole diff; this only decides what blocks.

- Write this bar into every reviewer prompt from the first round, local or CI, before any finding arrives.
- When a review reports, sort each finding against the bar before touching code. Fix only what passes it, plus the other copies of that same mistake (§ After a 🔴), with the smallest change, and add no features while fixing.
- After 3 red rounds in a row, stop patching: look up at least three ways others solved the same problem, compare them against each other, take the simplest one that removes the whole class, then continue. One search is a guess. Each step back that leaves the PR red leaves one round fewer before the next: research again after 2 more red rounds, then after every red round from the 6th on. From the 8th red round on, close to the hard stop, a step back looks up at least five ways instead of three.
- The 10th red round in a row is the hard stop: close the PR without merging, then rebuild the change from its base branch in a new PR, with that round's findings fixed in the rebuild and a `Rebuilds #<old number>` line in its body. The new PR starts its own count.
- A PR closed unmerged for good carries a label that says why: `dropped: no fix` when no fix was found, `dropped: not needed` when it has no reason left to exist. Create each label once with `gh label create`. The review counts read the line and the labels.

Without the bar, each fix adds surface for the next round to find, and the rounds never converge.

## PRs that edit the review workflow

The review app refuses its token to a run whose copy of `claude-code-review.yml` differs from the default branch's copy, so a review on such a PR can never be posted, and it must never start on them. Triage never reviews `claude-code-review.yml`, which it skips by name, so a PR whose only other files are skippable (Markdown, images and fonts outside the always-reviewed paths) is non-reviewable: the `Review gate` check passes without a review. That makes two rules:

- An edit to `claude-code-review.yml` ships in a PR of its own. Anything reviewable in the same PR (`claude.yml`, another workflow, the gate's scripts, `.claude/`, a `CLAUDE.md`, code) starts the review, whose post job is then refused the app's token ("The bot token exchange failed three times"), and the PR can never merge; split it. Edits to `claude.yml` alone get a normal review: it runs from the default branch's copy.
- No AI reviews such a PR in CI, so it is reviewed before merge, one of two ways:
  - **Every commit in it was written in the maintainer's own sessions:** two fresh subagents review the exact head commit that will merge. Neither is a fork of the session that wrote the change, and each gets only the PR's diff and its own prompt. One follows the review steps and the binary verdict rule of the routine-review prompt taken from the base branch's copy of `claude-code-review.yml`, never the PR's own copy. It runs the pre-screen's mechanical checks itself, since the CI pre-screen report does not exist locally. The other reviews as the deep tier, briefed to review the whole diff at that SHA adversarially under the binary verdict rule; the author may add focus points but never narrows that scope. Neither reviewer posts to the PR, applies a label or writes the deep-review trigger phrase; each returns its verdict to the author. Once both give 🟢, a PR comment records the head SHA and both verdict lines, and the merge passes `--match-head-commit <sha>` so it goes through only while that SHA is still the head. Any new commit re-runs both.
  - **Anything else,** including a PR the maintainer opened that carries someone else's commits: it merges only after the maintainer has read its whole diff.

### The first setup PR

The PR that first adds the review workflows has no gate on its base branch to pass: the `Review gate` check fails on it, and the review app refuses its token because the default branch holds no copy of `claude-code-review.yml` yet. So it targets the GitHub default branch, never `develop` when `develop` is not the default, and it is reviewed and merged as the workflow-only path above, with one change: the routine reviewer takes its prompt from the PR's own `claude-code-review.yml`, the files setup wrote, since the base has none. `.github/scripts/setup-review-gate.sh` creates and repairs no ruleset while the default branch lacks `.github/scripts/review_gate.py`, and names any ruleset that already requires `Review gate`: that check comes off until the merge, by the maintainer in the repo's settings. Once it merges, cascade it into `develop` when the project has one (push `develop` first if it exists only on this computer, so the script finds it on GitHub), then run `.github/scripts/setup-review-gate.sh` to protect both branches, and the same command with `--check` to confirm.

For any other failure, fix the cause.

## If the gate itself breaks

The gate runs the base branch's copy of `.github/scripts/review_gate.py` and `.github/review-gate.yml`, so a broken copy there fails the gate on every PR, the one that would fix it included. Only the maintainer recovers from that, and only for a PR that fixes those two files and changes nothing else but their tests and any copy the project keeps of them: it gets the two local 🟢 reviews of the section above, the maintainer takes `Review gate` off the branch's required checks (and `Evaluate review outcome`, where the branch still requires it, and `Claude On-Demand`, where a `checks: two` project requires it, since both wait on the same script) and merges it with `--match-head-commit <sha>`, then at once runs `.github/scripts/setup-review-gate.sh --branch <base>`, naming the PR's base branch (the one whose checks came off; `--branch` replaces the script's default branches), with `--require "<name>"` for each other check it took off, to require them again, and the same command with `--check` to confirm. Never for any other PR.

## Local session's job

Push, open the PR, watch the checks (see `token-efficiency.md`), and merge once every check has settled, the `Review gate` is 🟢 and every other required check passes. A PR whose base branch was changed, such as a stacked PR retargeted after its parent merged, starts no checks: push a commit or close and reopen it. If `needs-deep-review` appears but no deep review starts within a few minutes, report it instead of starting one yourself.

# Security

Nothing secret ships. Treat every artifact that leaves your hands as fully readable, reverse engineering included: app and game builds, web bundles and source maps, mobile packages, container images, public repos and their history. Obfuscation and packing slow a casual copier; they never hide a secret.

## Secrets

- No API keys, tokens, passwords, private or signing keys in the repo, a build or a config file that ships. They live server-side or in the platform's secret store (CI secrets, deploy-time environment, a vault), and code reads them at run time.
- A key a client must hold is public by definition. Give it the least power that works (one domain, read-only, rate-limited) and treat it as published.
- Never paste a secret into an issue, PR, commit message, log line, test fixture or chat. Use a placeholder such as `<API_KEY>`.
- A leaked secret is rotated first. Removing it from the history afterwards does not undo the leak.

## Before adding a credential or a download

- A new credential, account or token goes into the inventory: what it opens, where it lives, who can read it and how to rotate it. In a private repo that is `docs/security-posture.md`. In a public repo it is the private copy (ask the user where it lives), never the committed template.
- Anything the app downloads or loads at run time (updates, plugins, mods, remote config, user files) crosses a trust boundary: verify a signature or checksum, and parse it as untrusted input.

## Testing your own code's security

- Fuzzing, proof-of-concept exploits and other attack tests against the code this project runs are standard practice: its own parsers, sandboxes, file formats and protocols, the loaders for what users bring into it (mods, plugins, save files), and the libraries it bundles or installs. They find a hole before someone else does. Keep them in the project's tests or a git-ignored scratch folder.
- An attack test attacks only a copy of the code that the test starts itself, wherever the test runs (this computer or a build machine), or a test copy that the project's owner runs and set up for it. Never a live service, the project's own included: an attack there can corrupt real data or take the service down.
- Content people send or load into the project (bug reports, uploaded files, proposed changes, mods, save files) may be read and taken apart as untrusted input, including working out whether it carries an exploit.
- Out of scope: attacking any service or machine the project's owner does not run, such as another company's servers or a third-party API, their test copies included.
- When the assistant declines any part of this kind of work, in scope or not, it says so plainly and names the part it will not do, so the user decides what happens next. It never rewords the task, splits it into pieces or reaches for another tool to get past its own safeguards.

---
paths:
  - "README*"
  - "CHANGELOG*"

# Shipped text

Text a user reads (UI strings, docs, README, changelog, release notes, marketing copy, error messages) must read like a person wrote it. Code comments the compiler strips are out of scope.

- **No em dashes or en dashes.** Use a comma, parentheses, a colon, or two sentences.
- **No filler words:** "it's worth noting", "essentially", "robust", "seamless", "leverage", "delve", "comprehensive", "a testament to", "streamline", "empower", "elevate". The same applies to their equivalents in other languages the project ships.
- **No stock patterns:** forced groups of three, "not just X but Y", "it's not X, it's Y", closing summaries that repeat the paragraph.
- **Keep accuracy and the reason.** Plain is not bare: a first-time reader should understand what to do and why.

Before committing user-facing text, read it aloud. If it sounds like a press release, rewrite it.

# Task tracking

Any turn that will take three or more steps starts with `TaskCreate`, before the first work tool call. That covers the session plan once approved, any request with several items, multi-file refactors, and autonomous runs ("do what you think is best"). Skip it only for a single trivial action or pure conversation; when unsure, make the list.

- Mark a task `in_progress` the moment you start it and `completed` the moment it is done. Never work ahead of the list or batch status updates.
- One task in progress at a time, unless the work is explicitly parallel.
- A step discovered mid-run becomes a task immediately.
- For work split across several PRs, create one task per PR up front and chain them with `TaskUpdate({ taskId, addBlockedBy: [...] })` so the list follows the merge order.
- Autonomous runs still stop at visual checkpoints (`visual.md`) when a batch changes what people see.

If `TaskCreate` is not available (older builds, current models without `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`, or `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TASKS=0`), use the tasks mod's `mcp__tasks__taskmod_create`, `mcp__tasks__taskmod_update`, `mcp__tasks__taskmod_list` and `mcp__tasks__taskmod_get` when the session has them, which work the same way; otherwise use `TodoWrite` and express order by position. If neither tool exists, keep a numbered checklist in chat, update it every turn, and say once that the task tools are missing.

---
paths:
  - "**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx,mjs,cjs,py,go,rs,java,kt,kts,cs,c,cc,cpp,h,hpp,swift,dart,rb,php,gd,lua,ex,exs,scala}"

# Testing

A test is code the project pays for on every PR, so it ships only when it earns its place.

## When a test earns its place

1. It guards something a user would notice break, or a hard contract (a file or save format, a public API, determinism, thread safety).
2. It fails for one reason, and no other test in its file fails for that reason. Near copies merge into one table of named rows.
3. It checks the outcome, never the implementation: no pinning private constants, call counts or internal layout.
4. A check that the old, wrong version fails (a mutant check) only for a formula that already broke once, or for codecs, fixed-point math and determinism. Never by default.
5. A seeded sweep only where no boundary table can list the input: codecs, determinism, range invariants, and parsers or guards that read free-form text such as a shell command, where the spellings mix.
6. Benchmarks stay out of the pass or fail suite.
7. A test file stays lean: a PR that grows it says why.

Review blocks a new test that misses rules 1 to 3. `docs/test-audit.md` holds the method for checking an existing suite against this list.

## Test the real code

A test calls the production function. It never re-implements the logic in the test and checks the copy against itself, and it does not mock the unit under test. Mock only what the unit talks to (network, clock, disk) and only when the real thing is slow or unavailable.

## Cover the edges on purpose

- For logic with ranges or branches, write a table of cases: each boundary, one step either side of it, empty input and the largest supported input. Name every row, so a failure says which case broke.
- Where rule 5 allows a seeded randomized sweep, print the seed on failure so the case can be replayed.
- When fixing a bug, first add the test that fails on the old code, then fix. Keep that test.
- When replacing a formula that already broke once, keep a check that the case table still catches the old, wrong version. If the old version passes the table, the table is too weak.

## Tiers

- **Every PR:** fast tests only, a few minutes at most.
- **Nightly or weekly:** slow suites (long sweeps, integration, performance). A red scheduled run must open or update an issue, because nothing else will surface it.

## Coverage

Coverage is a report, never a merge gate. A gate rewards tests that execute lines without checking results. Use the report to find untested code worth testing.

## Flaky tests

A flaky test is a bug. Quarantine it in the same PR that notices it (skip with a linked issue), then fix it. Never re-run until green and merge.

# Token efficiency

## Find before you read

Locate a symbol before opening a file, then read only the function or section you need. `/find` (`.claude/skills/find/SKILL.md`) holds the lookup sequence for this project's code-research tool, **FindWright**, and when to fall back to Grep, Glob and Read.

Enable an MCP server only while the work needs it. Every enabled server adds its tool definitions to every message.

## Shell commands

- One command per call where you can. Permission rules match the whole command string, so `&&` chains prompt more and fail in confusing ways.
- Never retry a timed-out command with the same timeout. Builds and installs start at 420 000 ms. The first two retries add 180 000 ms each (600 000, then 780 000); every later retry adds 120 000 ms.

## Agent calls

Leave `model` and `effort` out of `Workflow` and agent calls, so they run on the session's model and effort. A pinned value overrides the person's choice.

When the `builder` agent is installed (`~/.claude/agents/builder.md`), hand it each feature or fix of about 20 lines or more that a test can prove: a brief with the goal, the files and the test command. It runs on a small, cheap model at the model and effort its own file pins, in this folder, so the project's rules still apply. Keep design, debugging an unknown cause and edits of a few lines in the main session. When it reports back, run the tests yourself, read the whole diff and check the result where it shows (the browser, the running app) before trusting it; the main session does every commit and push.

For a job that changes a web page, add the layout check to the brief's test command: `node "$HOME/.bindwright/helper/node_modules/bindwright/hooks/layout-check.mjs" <page URL>`, from the helper Bindwright's setup installs. It opens the page headless at phone and desktop width and fails on overlapping elements, text that overflows its box and sideways scroll, the misses a builder cannot see; it needs Node 22+ and Chrome, Chromium or Edge. Mark a deliberate overlap with `data-layout-ignore`.

## Watching CI

After every push, watch the PR's checks; never use `gh run watch`. When the `ci-watch` mod is loaded, it watches the PR after `git push` or `gh pr create` and wakes the session once all checks settle; follow the mod and start no second watcher. Otherwise use the **Monitor tool** where it exists:

- One monitor per PR, timeout one hour, so a stuck check becomes a loud timeout instead of a silent wait.
- Inside it, poll `gh pr checks <pr> --json name,bucket` about every 60 seconds. Filter on the `bucket` field with `gh`'s own `--jq` (the standalone `jq` binary is missing on some shells, and an empty result looks exactly like "still running").
- Print each check as it settles and finish with an explicit "all checks settled" line.
- On a new push to the same PR, stop the old monitor and start a new one.

Monitor is missing on some cloud providers and when non-essential traffic is disabled. Without it, run this as one Bash call with `run_in_background` and act when it exits. It stops after about nine minutes; if checks are still pending, run it again.

```bash
sleep 45
for i in $(seq 8); do
  state=$(gh pr checks <pr> --json bucket --jq 'if length == 0 then "none" else ([.[] | select(.bucket == "pending")] | length | tostring) end')
  [ "$state" = "0" ] && break
  sleep 60
done
gh pr checks <pr> --json name,bucket --jq '.[] | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"'
```

When everything is green, merge per `git.md` § Merging. On a red check, read the failing log (`gh run view <id> --log-failed`), fix it on the branch and push. Ask first only when the failure is ambiguous (flaky test, infrastructure outage, or the test and the change disagree about intended behavior).

### Fast path for docs-only PRs

Diffs of only Markdown, images and fonts outside the always-reviewed paths (the gate's own files, any `.claude/` folder, any `CLAUDE.md`, and `triage.always_review` in `.github/review-gate.yml`) pass the `Review gate` check without a review in about 30 seconds. Skip the monitor: wait about 90 seconds, check `gh pr view <pr> --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus`, then merge per `git.md` § Merging:

- `MERGEABLE` and `CLEAN`: merge.
- `BLOCKED` on a required approval: a reviewer other than the author approves it; until then, wait.
- Anything else: stop and report the state. Never merge past a rule.

Approval to open the PR covers this merge. A PR that changes `.github/workflows/claude-code-review.yml` gets no AI review in CI; it merges only as `review-tiers.md` § PRs that edit the review workflow describes.

## Long sessions

An approaching auto-compaction is no reason to stop, wrap up or close the session: keep working through it, mid-task included. Run the close-session ritual only when the maintainer asks for it, or when every task of the session is done and nothing is left to work on.

Without a hand-off that carries the work across a compaction (the `compact-handoff` mod is one), keep the task list current as the context fills, so the compaction's summary starts from where the work stands.

When responses slow down or degrade, the same file keeps getting re-read, or system reminders pile up, stop and reframe from the task list rather than push on.

## Scratch and build output

Scratch files, test copies and captures go in the session's scratchpad, or in the project's git-ignored build folder, never in a fixed folder such as `C:/tmp` or `/tmp`. The CLI deletes a session's scratchpad together with its transcript once both are older than `cleanupPeriodDays`, so anything worth keeping moves into the project before the session ends.

# Tracker

The work state lives in GitHub issues, not in the repo. The repo holds the rules; the issues hold where each piece of work stands.

The board is `advanced.trackerProject` in `.bindwright/project.json`, written `"<owner>/<number>"`. `null` means the project has no board: issues alone, with project status in a pinned issue (see Project status updates).

The issues live in this repo unless `advanced.trackerRepo` names another, written `"<owner>/<repo>"`: a private repo that keeps the work items apart from code that is public. Then every `gh issue` command below takes `--repo <that repo>`.

## Board visibility

The board holds the project's full engineering details, so it stays private. Before every board read (the open items, the newest status update), check its visibility: `gh project view <number> --owner <owner> --format json --jq .public`. When it prints `true`, open the reply with a plain warning, before anything else: the board is public, so anyone, crawlers included, can read its fields, status updates and item notes. The fix is `gh project edit <number> --owner <owner> --visibility PRIVATE`; a clean public copy (`advanced.publicRoadmap`) is the safe way to show outsiders the plan. Warn on every read, since the board can be made public on GitHub at any time. A public repo's issues are public whatever the board's setting, so a project with public code keeps its full-detail issues in a private `trackerRepo`.

## Work items

Every piece of work has an issue. Work found during a session gets a new one at once, from `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/work-item.md`, linked to its parent with a `Part of #N` line.

The issue body, not a comment thread, carries the state, so the latest state sits at the top of one page:

- `### Current state`: where the work stands, the next step, measurements and dead ends, newest first.
- When it grows long, older detail moves into the `Full history` block at the end of the body.
- An item on hold says so in a `Waits on:` line under its current state.

A PR body carries only its `Resolves #N` or `Part of #N` line (`Resolves <owner>/<repo>#N` when the issues live in a `trackerRepo`) and the usual What and Why. It never holds hand-off state.

## Project status updates

A status update says the project's state changed. It is not a session log. Post one only when:

1. A milestone, or a major arc of one, completes: health `COMPLETE`, with a short recap naming the issues and PRs, up to 150 words.
2. The health colour changes between `ON TRACK`, `AT RISK` and `OFF TRACK`.
3. The plan changes: a milestone goal is redefined, a date moves, or a direction call is made.

Most sessions post none. Shape, about 60 to 100 words:

```
## <headline> (<YYYY-MM-DD>)
- Health: <ON TRACK | AT RISK | OFF TRACK | COMPLETE>, <why: required for AT RISK and OFF TRACK>
- Plan: <what changed in the plan, or "unchanged">
```

The update's own status field matches its Health line. Root causes, file names and dead ends stay on the issues.

## Commands

Board commands need the `project` scope: `gh auth refresh -s project` adds it. Write every body to a file first and pass it with `--body-file`, or `-F body=@<file>` for `gh api`.

| Job | With a board | Without one |
|---|---|---|
| Open items | `gh project item-list <number> --owner <owner> --format json --limit 200`, in board order; when its `totalCount` is larger than the items it returned, run it again with a `--limit` above that count. Skip items whose `status` is `Done`, those whose `content.type` is not `Issue` (pull requests, drafts), those whose `content.repository` is not the tracker repo (`advanced.trackerRepo`, or this one when it is `null`: `gh repo view --json nameWithOwner -q .nameWithOwner`; a board can span repos, and the commands below act on that one), and issues the read below shows closed | `gh issue list --state open --assignee @me --limit 1000` (without `--limit` it stops at 30); when it returns exactly 1000, run it again with a higher `--limit` |
| Read an item | `gh issue view <n> --json title,state,body,labels` | Same |
| Update its state | `gh issue edit <n> --body-file <file>` | Same |
| New item | `gh issue create --assignee @me --title <title> --body-file <file>`, then `gh project item-add <number> --owner <owner> --url <issue url>` | The same `gh issue create`; the `--assignee @me` is what lets the open-items list find it |
| Newest status update | `gh api graphql -f query='query($o:String!,$n:Int!){repositoryOwner(login:$o){... on ProjectV2Owner{projectV2(number:$n){id statusUpdates(first:1,orderBy:{field:CREATED_AT,direction:DESC}){nodes{createdAt status body}}}}}}' -f o=<owner> -F n=<number>`; the order must be explicit, since `last:1` without it returns the oldest | The newest comment on the pinned `Project status` issue |
| Post a status update | The query above gives the board's `id`; then `gh api graphql -f query='mutation($p:ID!,$s:ProjectV2StatusUpdateStatus!,$b:String!){createProjectV2StatusUpdate(input:{projectId:$p,status:$s,body:$b}){statusUpdate{id}}}' -f p=<id> -f s=<ON_TRACK, AT_RISK, OFF_TRACK or COMPLETE> -F b=@<file>` | `gh issue comment <status issue> --body-file <file>`; create and pin the issue (`gh issue pin`) the first time |

Offline or signed out, say the tracker cannot be read and plan from git alone. At close, write what could not be posted (each issue's new current state, any status update) to `.bindwright/pending-tracker.md`, and the first time add that path to the file `git rev-parse --git-path info/exclude` prints, so no commit picks it up; the next `/start-session` posts it once the tracker answers, then deletes the file.
files..claude/rules/visual.md:
# Visual work

Applies to anything whose correctness depends on what a person sees: web or native UI, games, charts, design tools.

## One slice at a time

A slice is the smallest change a person can check with one short yes/no checklist. If you cannot write that checklist, the slice is too big (or has no visual surface, and this rule does not apply).

Build a visual feature in this order, checking each step before the next:

1. Data, with unit tests only.
2. A placeholder on the real surface (a visible dummy element) to prove it renders.
3. Real data shown plainly.
4. Real styling.
5. Live updates when the data or route changes.
6. Tests and cleanup.

When a step fails, the problem is in that step, and the previous one is the rollback point. Never bundle several visual systems into one PR.

## Iterate locally, push once

1. Run the tests plus `/verify` when the project has `.claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md`, otherwise a headless start, then commit on the feature branch. Report and stop.
2. The maintainer checks the visuals.
3. On a regression, keep iterating locally without pushing.
4. Once the maintainer confirms, push and open the PR, and add "Visual check confirmed <date>" to its Notes.

Silence is not approval. Do not push a visual slice until the maintainer says it looks right. Review fixes that do not change visuals push as usual.

## Checklists, never "check for regressions"

Give the maintainer concrete yes/no items tied to the change:

| Change | Checklist |
|---|---|
| Config flip, no intended visual change | The app starts, renders at every size, and logs no errors. |
| New visual element | One line per thing it newly shows or does. |
| Copy change | The new text appears where expected and fits without clipping. |
| Bug fix | "Do X, expect Y." |

## Reuse before building

Before creating a UI component, check the project's shared components. If a suitable one is missing, add it there first, then use it.

## Not covered

Pure logic with unit-testable results, refactors with no visual change, and docs or CI changes.

files..claude/skills/close-session/SKILL.md:
---
name: close-session
description: Close a work session. Verifies what is really finished, commits, lands the work, cleans up and hands off to the next session. Use when the maintainer asks for it, or when every task of the session is done; never just because the context is filling up.
---

# /close-session

Run the steps in order without asking between them. Stop and ask only before a force-push, deleting a branch that holds unmerged work, or rewriting history someone else has pulled. If `.claude/rules/visual.md` exists and this session changed what people see, do not push until the maintainer has confirmed the visual check.

## Verify what is done

Only when this session claims a feature or milestone complete. Re-read its definition of done (its issue, ROADMAP, design doc or PR description) and mark each item:

- ✅ **verified**: seen working in the running app, with the commit, the screen or route, and a screenshot or log where it applies;
- ⚠️ **partial**: works in some cases; list the gaps;
- ❌ **unmet**: open a follow-up and stop claiming completion.

When `.claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md` exists, say for each change people can see or use whether `/verify` passed before its last commit; one it never ran before is ⚠️ at best.

One ❌ means the feature is not complete. If an item stopped making sense mid-way, change the definition of done in its own commit first; never quietly call a gap "deferred".

## Derived docs

Update `README.md` or `CLAUDE.md` when this session changed what they describe, and say which sections changed.

Then check the living docs are still current: for each behaviour, name, path, command or number the session's diff changed, search `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/` and `.claude/rules/` for the old wording, and fix every claim that no longer holds. Dated records (released changelog entries, dated notes) stay as written. `docs/docs-audit.md` covers a full sweep.

## Code-research count

Run `python3 .claude/scripts/research-adherence.py` from the repo root (`python` on Windows). It reads the transcript and compares calls to FindWright with plain code searches that carry no bypass marker: Grep and Glob calls, and shell commands that start with a recursive search. Searches of docs, logs and data, and filters on another command's output, do not count. Report its line. Below 70% means the next session starts by finding out why.

## FindWright hit rate

When `$HOME/.findwright/helper/node_modules/findwright/src/cli.mjs` exists and `node --version` shows 22.16 or later on the 22 line, or 24 or later, run `node "$HOME/.findwright/helper/node_modules/findwright/src/cli.mjs" hits` from the repo root; otherwise say the hit rate is not recorded on this computer, and why, and go on. It scores this session's FindWright searches (a hit when the file the session opened next was in the answer), records the figure in `.findwright/hits.jsonl` and prints `{rate, scored, goal, assess}`. Report the rate against the goal (90% unless `.findwright/config.json` sets `goal`). When it also prints `saved`, add one line from it: with `saved.main` set, "and you saved an estimated $<main> in the main session and $<helpers> in helper sessions", said as an estimate that counts only the extra turns a missed search costs, so it errs low; with `saved.main` null, say the saving is not measurable yet and give `saved.why`. Name each model in `saved.unpriced` as left out of the estimate. When `assess` is true, the last three sessions all fell short: run the same command with `assess`, explain each cause and suggested change in plain words, and apply a change to `.findwright/config.json` only on the user's yes.

## Pruning pass

Rules, tests and memory only ever grow, and a long rule file is where a session reads past a rule. So at most once a month, offer to prune. The date of the last pass, offered or run, lives in this clone's git config, which its worktrees share and no commit carries: `git config --local bindwright.lastPruning` prints it, and `git config --local bindwright.lastPruning <YYYY-MM-DD>` sets it. When it prints nothing, set today's date and skip this step, so the first offer comes a month after the first close that runs it; when it is less than 30 days old, skip this step. Otherwise ask once: "It has been a month: look for rules, tests and memory entries nothing uses any more?" On a no, set today's date and go on.

On a yes, list the candidates, each with one line on why:

- Rule text in `.claude/rules/` and `CLAUDE.md` that repeats another file, or names a file, command or setting that no longer exists.
- Tests that are skipped for good, or that fail for the same reason as another test in their file (`.claude/rules/testing.md`, rule 2).
- Memory entries in `~/.claude/projects/<project-slug>/memory/` that name a file or function that no longer exists, repeat another entry, or say what the repo's rules already say.

This is a report only: write nothing for it, in the repo, the tracker or anywhere else, and leave what to do with each candidate to the user. Then set today's date.

## Project steps

If `.bindwright/session-steps.md` lists "Extra close steps", run them now, except those marked *after the hand-off*: they run at the end, before the last message.

## Commit and PR

Stage the session's files by name, never `git add -A` or `git add .`. A file `git status` lists that this session did not change stays out of the commit; name it in the last message. Then take the first row that matches:

| Situation | Do |
|---|---|
| Branch goal not finished | Commit the work. No PR. |
| `hotfix/*` finished | PR to `main`. After it merges, open the cascade PR: a `chore/cascade-<name>` branch from `origin/develop` that merges `origin/main` with `--no-ff`, into `develop`. Done only when the cascade merges. |
| `release/*` finished | Same as a hotfix: PR to `main`, tag the release commit, then cascade. |
| Any other branch finished | Commit, open a PR to `develop`, watch the checks, merge once every check has settled and the required ones pass. |

Commit and PR format, `--body-file`, merge style and branch cleanup are in `git.md`; watching checks is in `token-efficiency.md`. Run each post-merge command as its own call.

## Hand-off in the tracker

After the commit and PR, so the state records how they ended. For each issue this session worked on, rewrite its `### Current state` per `.claude/rules/tracker.md`: where the work stands, decisions made and why, what the next session should do first. Work without an issue gets one now with the "New item" command, a branch with no PR included. Rules and conventions stay in `.claude/rules/`; session figures (the code-research count, context use) stay in the chat.

Then post a project status update only when this session completed a milestone or a major arc of one, changed the health colour, or changed the plan; `tracker.md` § Project status updates has the shape. Most sessions post none.

## Hand-off file

Rewrite `.bindwright/handoff.md`. It stays in this checkout, out of git: the first time, add the line `.bindwright/handoff.md` to the file `git rev-parse --git-path info/exclude` prints (a worktree shares it with its main checkout, but keeps its own hand-off file). It only points at the tracker, in at most ten lines, and never restates an issue's state:

```
# Hand-off (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM)
- Worked on: #12 (PR #40 waiting on review), #15
- Start with: #13
- Open question: <one line, or none>
```

## Steps after the hand-off

Run the extra close steps marked *after the hand-off*, if any: they read this session's finished work and its hand-off.

## Last message

> **Session closed.** Everything is committed; [PR #N merged and branches deleted | branch pushed, PR #N waiting on checks | work committed locally on `<branch>`]. Start a fresh conversation for the next session.
files..claude/skills/find/SKILL.md:
---
name: find
description: Locate code before reading or editing it. Use whenever the user asks "where is X", "what calls Y", "find usages of Z", or whenever you need to find a symbol, function, type or pattern yourself.
---

# /find

The lookup sequence for this project's code-research tool, **FindWright** (https://github.com/starfoxcom/findwright). Follow it in order and stop at the first useful result. Read only the range you found, never the whole file.

## Sequence

1. `find` with a plain-English question, a name, or both: the files that answer it, best first.
2. `search` with one or more regexes, optional `globs` and `context`: every matching line, with the symbol around it. It covers every file the project tracks, Markdown, config and templates included.
3. `symbols` to look a name up by kind (function, class, heading, key).
4. `outline` with a path: its symbols and line ranges, to read only the part you need.
5. `coverage` when a file seems missing: what the index reads and which files yield no symbol.

The index updates itself on every call. Its symbols come from the rules in `.findwright/config.json`: when `coverage` shows files the work searches with no symbol, run `/findwright:fit`, which writes the rules that name them.

## Falling back to Grep and Glob

Allowed only when:

- FindWright returned nothing usable for two differently worded queries;
- the target is not code (Markdown, config, binaries, ignored files);
- FindWright is unavailable for this scope.

Say which condition applies. For a shell `grep` or `rg`, add the comment `# FINDWRIGHT_BYPASS: <reason>` to the command so the close-session count treats it as a deliberate fallback.

## Citing

Name the call that found it, in one line:

> Found `parseHeader` via `<call>` at `src/codec/header.ts:42`.
files..claude/skills/start-session/SKILL.md:
---
name: start-session
description: Start a work session. Reads the project state and git state, then proposes a plan and waits for approval. Use at the start of every session, or when the user says "session start", "let's start" or "ready to work".
---

# /start-session

Planning only. Create no branches and change no files in this turn, apart from the session's purpose note in step 4 where it applies.

## 1. Read

- The tracker, with the commands in `.claude/rules/tracker.md`: the open items (in progress first, then the next in queue, and items on hold apart with what each waits on), and the newest project status update. An item's `### Current state` is the last session's hand-off; it outranks anything re-derived from git.
- `.bindwright/pending-tracker.md`, if it exists: writes an offline close could not post (`tracker.md`). Read them as part of the hand-off, post them once the plan is approved, then delete the file.
- Ask of that status update: is its colour still true, given the board and what this session finds? If not, the colour has changed: say so in the report, and post the new update once the plan is approved.
- `.bindwright/handoff.md`, if it exists: the last session's pointers in this checkout. Read it first, then the issues it names; where they disagree, the issues win.
- `.bindwright/session-steps.md` if it exists: its "Extra start steps" run after the git checks below.

If the focus is unclear from the user's message or the current branch, ask before reading further.

## 2. Check git

Run these as separate calls, in parallel:

- `git status`
- `git branch --show-current`
- `git log --oneline -10`
- `git fetch --prune origin`, then `git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/develop` (how far behind the current branch is)
- `gh pr list --author @me --state open`

Then run the extra start steps, if any.

Last, Bindwright's own check. In `plugins/installed_plugins.json` in the Claude config folder (`$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, or `~/.claude`), take the `bindwright` install that applies here: the one whose `projectPath` is this repo root, otherwise the one with `scope` `managed` or `user`; never one whose `projectPath` names another folder. Skip the step when the most specific settings file that sets that plugin's `enabledPlugins` entry (the managed settings an administrator installs, then `.claude/settings.local.json`, then `.claude/settings.json`, then `settings.json` in the config folder) sets it to `false`: a plugin turned off in `/plugin` stays installed. Otherwise run `node "$HOME/.bindwright/helper/node_modules/bindwright/hooks/notice.mjs" --plugin "<installPath>"` from the repo root. At most once a day it prints a line when the plugin, its helper or this repo's Bindwright files are behind; put any line it prints at the top of the report. It prints nothing otherwise. Run it outside the Bash sandbox when one is on: inside it the opt-in counts send cannot reach the network. A missing or unreadable file, plugin, helper or Node skips the step without a word, with one exception: when a `bindwright` install applies here and is not turned off, the helper is missing, and `bindwright/counts.json` in the Claude config folder holds `"share": true` with an entry for this repo whose `kind` is set, put one line at the top of the report instead: this computer turned the review counts on, but they are not being sent while Bindwright's helper is missing, and `/bindwright:setup` installs it again.

## 3. Report, in this order

1. **Project status:** current focus, open work, blockers.
2. **Git status:** current branch, uncommitted changes, how far behind `develop` it is, open PRs. If `develop` has moved ahead, propose merging it in before resuming: `git fetch origin`, then `git merge origin/develop` on the work branch.
3. **Branch:** if the work needs a new branch, propose its name per `git.md` and ask before creating it.
4. **Areas touched:** the directories the plan will change. Anything outside the branch's scope becomes a prerequisite branch that lands first; name it.
5. **Plan:** the ordered steps, with dependencies. Three to seven steps; split anything larger into another session.

## 4. Stop

When the session-title hook named a purpose file at the start of this session (Bindwright's global `session-title` extra), write this session's purpose to that file before ending the turn: what the plan works on, in 10 words at most and as few as will do, without the project's name. That is the one file this turn writes. From the next prompt, the one that approves the plan, the session's title reads `<Project> - <purpose>`. Rewrite the file when the user corrects the plan or the session's focus changes.

End the turn after the report. Once the user approves or corrects the plan, create the tasks per `.claude/rules/task-tracking.md` and start.

# Settings for the review gate (.github/scripts/review_gate.py). Every value
# starts at the gate's default; delete a line to keep the default.
# Unknown keys and bad values fail the gate instead of being ignored.
# The workflows read this file from the PR's base branch, so a PR cannot
# change the settings its own review runs under.

# The "Review gate" check is always reported. "two" also keeps the older
# "Claude On-Demand" check up to date, for branch rules that still require
# it; "one" once they require "Review gate" alone.
checks: one

# The runner label (runs-on) for the review jobs; several labels, comma
# separated, pick a self-hosted runner ("self-hosted, linux"). Run such a
# runner under an account of its own with no Claude Code setup: the
# reviewers load that account's user settings, hooks and instructions.
# On a Linux runner (WSL counts) without a Linux Node 22 or newer and
# npm, each review job downloads the
# official Node build into its temp folder, checked against a pinned
# checksum, to install the CLI.
runner: ubuntu-latest

# The review that runs on every PR with reviewable files. Its backup runs
# once when the attempts on its own model fail, a usage limit included.
routine:
  model: claude-fable-5-2
  effort: low
  max_turns: 120
  fallback_model: claude-opus-5-5
  fallback_effort: high

# The deeper review the routine one asks for on risky diffs.
deep:
  model: claude-fable-5-2
  effort: medium
  max_turns: 120
  fallback_model: claude-opus-5-5
  fallback_effort: high

# The backup a tier uses when its own fallback_model or fallback_effort
# line is left out.
fallback:
  model: claude-opus-5-5
  effort: high

# A folder of the project's own pre-screen checks (*.py and *.sh), run from
# the base branch with the changed-file list; their output joins the review
# context, and a check that exits non-zero is reported as a violation.
# A check that runs the PR's code can fake its own report, and on a
# self-hosted runner that is not wiped between jobs it can leave files or
# processes behind for the review; keep such checks on hosted or one-job
# runners. Empty: none.
# attribution: on scans the lines a PR adds for AI-attribution markers
# (co-author lines, "generated with" footers, session links), and the
# reviewer checks the commits and the PR body for them; off skips both.
prescreen:
  dir:
  attribution: on

# The project's own deep-review triggers, on top of the gate's: path globs
# (comma separated, any case; `*` crosses folders, a trailing `/` covers a
# folder), and a Python regex matched against the lines a PR adds (no `#`,
# which starts a comment here; one pair of outer quotes is dropped, so wrap a
# regex that starts and ends with the same quote in another pair). They
# apply to PRs the gate reviews: a PR of only skippable files (Markdown,
# images, fonts outside the always-reviewed paths) passes without a review,
# so a trigger on such a file never fires; list its path under
# triage.always_review too. Empty: none.
# auto: on lets the routine review ask for the deep review by itself: on
# these triggers, on the gate's own files, and when it judges one needed.
# off: it starts none by itself and the triggers are not used; a person
# asks for one with `@claude review this PR` on each push that needs it,
# or adds the needs-deep-review label so every later push gets one.
escalate:
  auto: on
  paths:
  patterns:

# Paths that always get a review, whatever their file type, on top of the
# gate's own (.github/scripts/, .github/review-guide.md, any .claude/
# folder, any CLAUDE.md): globs as for escalate.paths. Without this, a PR
# of only Markdown, images or fonts passes without a review.
triage:
  always_review:

# Extra tools both reviewers may use, comma separated: Bash(...) patterns,
# Read, Grep or Glob. A Bash pattern that runs the PR's code hands that code
# the review's tokens; add one only when that is acceptable. Empty: none.
reviewer:
  allowed_tools:
